speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext:
Dr. Koester, I wish to inform the House that His Excellency the Governor General has seen fit to authorize this Chamber to proceed with the election of a Speaker.
This decision is of vital importance to the proper conduct of this Assembly. Without a firm and enlightened Speaker, our parliamentary democracy would not be viable. Canadians depend on their Members of Parliament to defend the causes they hold dear. As we all know, opposing views, especially when they are firmly rooted, often cause the business of Parliament to be conducted in an atmosphere of antagonism.
It is then up to the Speaker to maintain order while remaining fair and impartial, to allow the majority to govern while at the same time giving dissenting voices an equal chance to make themselves heard.

This is a tough job description for what is not always a popular role. In Great Britain Speakers have been hanged and beheaded.

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext: Prime Ministers too!

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext:
Thankfully, here in Canada we have been less extreme in demonstrating our unhappiness with the system. We have yelled at a few Speakers, insulted one or two, and more recently nearly deafened one with bell ringing. Yet for all of that, because of the calibre and wisdom of those who have held this high post, we have generally treated our Speakers with the respect and gratitude which the office deserves.
Today it gives me great pleasure to nominate our colleague from Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) for this somewhat overwhelming responsibility. He is a House of Commons veteran who has experienced both the satisfaction and the many frustrations of parliamentary life.

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST

I hope the House will become more serious when we have a serious Speaker. For the Hon. Member quite simply there is no finer life, whether he be passionately pleading the concerns of his constituents or fighting for the traditions of this institution. The Member for Ottawa West has devoted the past 30 years to public service in this community and to federal politics. He has done so with a sense of duty, understanding, and a special quality of kindness which, in our view, makes him an admirable candidate for Speaker. His most recent discharging of responsibilities in the Chair as Deputy Speaker demonstrated an effective use of his abilities.
Finally, Members may not know that our candidate brings another accomplishment to the job. During the Second World War he served in the RCAF as an air navigator. I would recommend that he dust off those old navigational skills; they may hold him in good stead in the days to come.
[ Translation]
I move, seconded by the Hon. Leader of the Opposition, that the Hon. Lloyd Francis, Member for the Electoral District of Ottawa West, do take the Chair of this House as Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Mulroney (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext:
Dr. Koester, this is an important time transitionally for Members of the House of Commons.

The election of a new Speaker of the House of Commons is due to the resignation of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides, Madame Sauve, who served the House with unequalled dignity and energy. She has left her mark with respect to parliamentary procedure and the day-to-day administration of the House of Commons. Naturally, we are sorry to lose her, but we are convinced that, in her new role as Governor General, Madame Sauve will continue to use her abilities and her competence to serve honourably the people of Canada and to defend the best interests of our country.

Members of the House of Commons are assembled here today to make what is arguably the most important decision that is required of any of us in the course of our duties in the House of Commons on behalf of the people of Canada. The election of the Speaker of the House of Commons is important, not only because it is a prerequisite for the conduct of

January 16, 1984
Election of Speaker
business in this place, but because the choice that we will make today will influence both the quality and the shape of debate in the House and will necessarily have an impact on our lives, both as Members of Parliament and as Canadians.
I am certain that all of who have served in the Chair over the years, including the most recent occupant, would attest to the fact that the job of Speaker is a very difficult and challenging one, made doubly so by the fact that the House of Commons is a place of great partisanship. However, it is a partisanship, as I have learned in my own very limited experience, which is bound by, and expressed within, the strict and equitable exercise of our rules. This notion, this indispensable notion, must prevail at all times.
In a democracy progress clearly results from forceful debate and intense scrutiny here in the House of Commons. When we ignore or abuse the rules of this place, as I suspect, Dr. Koester, we all have in varying degrees from time to time, we turn our backs on the achievements of the past and the promises of the future. It is for this reason that we gather in assemblies such as this to elect a Speaker.
This is a moment of remarkable importance in our parliamentary life. The person chosen to act in the role as first commoner is charged with the responsibility of acting as the conscience of the House and as interpreter and arbiter when disputes arise here in the House. The Speaker is guardian of the rules, the practices, and most of all in that important responsibility, must be above partisanship at all times but particularly when we are told, Dr. Koester, that there is a possibility that there will be an election this year or some year.

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this occasion I would like to say a few words on the nomination which is before the House for the selection of a new Speaker. In so doing I would like to comment briefly on our previous Speaker and say something about the process for selecting Speakers in general.
As has been indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney), the position of Speaker of the House of Commons is supremely important not only for Members of the House but, because of all the duties connected thereto, for the people of Canada in our system of parliamentary democracy.
The Speaker, whoever he or she may be, is responsible in the final analysis not simply to the government which basically proposes the name of the Speaker under our present system but fundamentally responsible to all Members of the House of Commons.
[ Translation]
And it is in that context that I want to emphasize the work done by Madame Sauve in the past. As Speaker, she made very difficult rulings in this Parliament, particularly during the constitutional debate. That was obvious. During that period, as Speaker, she ruled in favour of the House of Commons, not simply in favour of the Government. During that very trying period in the House, she also made some rulings which went against the Government. And in other circumstances, some of her rulings went against the views of the Opposition. Madame Sauve was an exceptional Speaker and I wanted to say so.
I would now simply like to add that we in our Party will certainly be giving the new Speaker our full support and we wish him well in his onerous duties in this House. Anything I now have to say I want to make clear has nothing to do with the personality of Lloyd Francis, who I am sure will do a good job.
For the occasion, however, I would like to take this opportunity to remind the House of Commons that a committee of this House representing all Parties not long ago made a recommendation for the selection of Speaker, a selection very different from the process now being used. The committee of the House took into account the responsibilities of the Speaker to all Members of the House and made a recommendation that that committee, consisting of Liberals, Conservatives and New Democrats, thought would meet the responsibilities of the Speaker better than the current process. I as leader of my Party want to indicate very clearly that we agree with that recommendation.
The recommendation was that in order to enhance the moral authority of the Speaker as being responsible to all Members of the House and not simply to a government-and governments change from time to time, even in this country-it would be desirable to have the Speaker elected by secret ballot by all Members of the House. Therefore, a key recommendation was that instead of the Speaker's name being proposed by the Prime Minister of the day and, as has been our tradition, seconded by the Official Opposition, supported as a matter of routine as well by the New Democratic Party, the committee said that the Speaker should be directly elected by secret ballot by all Members of the House.
We in our Party think that process would be much better. If it were followed in the future, as we hope it will be, the Speaker so elected will have more moral authority in speaking to all Members of the House. This would enhance the position of individual Members, especially back-bench Members of the House of Commons. In that respect we think the recommend-
January 16, 1984

ed process would be an improvement. The Speaker's position, in short, would be enhanced and the power of the House of Commons, vis-a-vis the executive branch of the government, we think would also be enhanced.
1 want to conclude by saying that the present nominee has our full support, but I also urge future governments, whoever they may be, to pay attention to the all-Party recommendation which set out a more democratic and more effective process of electing a Speaker for this body.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to exercise my right as a back-bencher to take part in this debate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in his speech this morning about former Speakers being hanged, drawn and quartered, or whatever, to protect the rights of Parliament, and the Prime Minister is right about that. They were doing so, as 1 understand my British history, to defend the rights of Members of Parliament from the king. When King Charles entered the British House of Commons, Mr. Speaker Lenthall protected the Members so John Pym and other Members could retreat to the back of the House and get away by sailing down the River Thames. That is an honourable tradition.
We have replaced the king by the Prime Minister, it seems, in our system.

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST

speechtext:
There is room for only one emperor in Ottawa, I suppose!
In the previous system, before the imperial Prime Minister, the king never appointed the Speaker of the House of Commons. The House of Commons made sure it appointed its own Speaker. That was the beginning of our parliamentary democracy in Canada.
Why, then, are we in this House giving up our collective right to have a real election, not this farce of an election, by having our Members nominate candidates for Speaker rather than the Prime Minister? It seems to me that would make a lot of sense. When I suggested this in a letter to Members of the House last week, one of the Prime Minister's people said that it would turn things into a popularity contest. That is the view of those people of democracy and that is how far the imperial Prime Minister has got in our system.
[DOT] (U20)
I am sorry Hon. Members of the House have not taken the opportunity we had today to have a real election, to suggest a number of names. There are a number of competent people in the House who could be Speaker. I say this not as an attack on the nominee's credibility and competence, but as an attack on the system of choosing a Speaker. When it comes to the next
Election of Speaker
election of Speaker, which I think could be soon, I hope Hon. Members of the House of Commons will have more collective guts than they have shown today.
The Clerk of the House declared the motion carried in the affirmative, and Lloyd Francis, Esquire, Member for the electoral district of Ottawa West, duly elected to the Chair of the House.
Mr. Francis was conducted from his seat in the House to the Speaker's chair by the Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau and Mr. Brian Mulroney.

subtopic: MR. LLOYD FRANCIS, MEMBER FOR THE ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF OTTAWA WEST
speechtext:
Hon. Members, I beg to return my humble acknowledgements to the House for the great honour you have been pleased to confer upon me by choosing me to be your Speaker.

Hon. Members, I beg to return my humble acknowledgements to the House for the great honour you have been pleased to confer on me by choosing me to be your Speaker.

I would like to express my thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for nominating me to this illustrious office. I am deeply appreciative of the fact that the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) seconded the motion and of the kind words expressed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent).
I know that no Speaker can perform his duties without support from all sides of the House. I am touched and grateful to have received such warm best wishes. Having occupied the Chair as your Deputy Speaker for three years, I am heartened that your sentiments of trust and goodwill have survived my apprenticeship for this great honour.
I would like to pay tribute to my distinguished predecessor, Madam Sauve. I think we would all agree that this has been an active Parliament with much controversial legislation. Throughout these busy years, Madam Sauve distinguished herself by her composure, her sense of humour and her charm. Her work in response to the comments of the Auditor General and the Commissioner of Official Languages brought commendations from both of them. She also demonstrated that necessary prerequisite of any good Speaker: impartiality. These qualities, I am sure, will serve her well and benefit the whole nation when she assumes her new role as Governor General.

I am very conscious of the fact that by taking on the duties of Speaker of the House, I am taking part in a historic tradition that lives on and has proved its worth. I truly believe that this tradition owes a large part of its success to the rules that govern our parliamentary proceedings and are the culmination of many years of experience.
Since our Standing Orders are based on a common sense principle, the role of the Speaker is to ensure and maintain the proper conduct of the proceedings of this House. To many, it

January 16, 1984
Election of Speaker
may seem that our rules are both archaic and complex. In reality, however, they have been formulated as a response to any situations that may arise. This is absolutely necessary, since the House is a deliberative assembly that symbolizes the diverging opinions of all Canadians. The task of the Speaker is to guarantee impartial application of the Standing Orders, for the greater benefit of all Members. It is a difficult task and a great challenge. That is why traditionally, Speakers are always escorted to the chair after their election.
The Speaker is also responsible for the preservation of the dignity of this Chamber. No Speaker can do this without the trust and co-operation of all Members. I hope that in the heat of the moment you will not abandon your trust in me and feel that I have occasionally ruled against you. I hope you will remember my need for your co-operation when my impartiality does not give universal satisfaction.
In return for your trust in me, I pledge to do my utmost to be worthy of your trust; to perform my duties in the best tradition of the Speakership; to be truly impartial and fair to all; to protect the right of the majority to transact the business of the House while protecting the right of the minority to be heard; to give to each Member the same respect and consideration; to maintain order and decorum; and to observe the spirit of the rules of procedure and parliamentary life. I pledge to you that I will try to remember at all times that the Speaker is only the servant of this House and not its master, and I will endeavour to place these duties above every other consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that Bill C-3, An Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to amend and repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, with your leave, since I am the first Member of this House to rise in debate immediately following your inauguration as Speaker of this House, I wish to congratulate you, to extend my best wishes and to remind the House, as this was not mentioned before, that before entering politics you had been a senior official of my Department, and through you, I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to salute all those people working behind the scenes whom we do not necessarily know and who, especially at Health and Welfare Canada, have helped to realize the programs we have today and of which we are so proud, and especially the Health Insurance Program which is the subject of this debate. I have
January 16, 1984

heard you did very good work, and from time to time I find documents with your signature. Now we are colleagues. Today, you have become that impartial person who will preside over our destiny.

1 would like to say to all my colleagues that it is both with pleasure and regret that 1 am taking this opportunity to speak today on second reading of Bill C-3, the new Canada Health Act. I regret that the federal Government had to take this measure in order to stop the growing erosion of medicare and I regret, in a way, that the excellent recommendations of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall were rejected back in September of 1980 by the provinces at the federal-provincial conference in Winnipeg. I also regret, I must admit, that a year later, despite hundreds of briefs and very clear recommendations in the report of the Breau parliamentary task force, which was conducted by my colleague, the Hon. Member from New Brunswick, the provinces were not convinced to ban extra charges. A few years ago, in 1978, extra charges were in the amount of $50 million to $55 million. When I tabled the Bill in early December of last year, this amount had already grown to $100 million over the amount Canadians have already paid and this has hit them at a time when they are less prepared for it.
To sum up the so-called problems of medicare-the political confrontations and controversies which did take place in the past but which are fading away today-some players could accuse the federal Government of moving too fast. However, only history will tell; we do not know. One thing that is sure, which everyone knows, particularly the senior civil servants in all the provinces who have created medicare and who have given Canadians the excellent system we have, is that there is a serious problem which will have to be addressed sooner or later. An erosion of medicare is taking place and, of course, in the case of erosion, no one knows when it will make the house collapse. Therefore, the federal Government decided that the time to act was now.
The charges are increasing and becoming serious, but are not yet too disruptive from the viewpoint of the global system of medicare. We may be in too much of a hurry, but I do not believe so. I feel most Canadians do not believe we are. I believe that is the only accusation which could ever be made against Bill C-3.
There are many things which must be said under dossier and Hon. Members will excuse me if my remarks are perhaps delivered en vrac. I did not, for obvious reasons, have time to write a speech. I crossed the country last week from coast to coast. On Monday I met with the Minister of Health of Newfoundland in his capital city of St. John's. I met with the Minister of Health of Prince Edward Island in Charlottetown, and I met with eight of my provincial colleagues and one of my territorial colleagues in all of the five working days of last week. We had, I must say, excellent meetings. They were very positive. For the first time in a long while we got down to business, we were able to speak of medicare and of the draft regulations which I received on Monday at the same time they
Canada Health Act
received mine from me. We began to address the practical consequences of this new Canada Health Act which the House is studying today.
This Bill, I must say with great pride, having tested it and worked with it in a very intensive fashion all of last week, is a very good piece of legislation. That was confirmed to be by several players in the field. The provincial, federal and territorial people acknowledged it as a very good piece of legislation. Perhaps I should add at this point, Mr. Speaker, that the two provincial Ministers I have not yet met with I will meet in the coming days. They are outside the country right now. The territorial Minister of the Northwest Territories will soon be appointed-if he has not been appointed already-and I will meet with him as soon as possible, of course. However, together with the vast majority of my other colleagues, I had a chance to get down to business and talk of health.
The Act is a very good piece of legislation. Two words worried the provinces a lot. With my provincial colleagues I undertook eventually to replace them with better words. Although they are not new words or new concepts, in 1984 they may appear to place undue burdens on the provinces. Needless to say, this was not the intent of the Act. 1 will quickly give these words to my colleagues and to the Opposition. The provinces are very nervous about the words "adequate" and "reasonable" in Clause 12 of the Bill where one is applied to compensation for doctors and the other to budgets for hospitals. Reasonable compensation for doctors is in the existing legislation and we all agree with the idea; there is no doubt about that. Adequate funding for hospitals is not word for word in the existing legislation but has been with us for 25 years through another phrase. However, the words may appear to carry a notion of value judgment which is not intended and may appear to groups and communities as a tool to have a tribunal assess what province x, y, or z has granted them.
As my officials and myself have explained to our provincial colleagues, there is a long-standing tradition which explains what is meant by reasonable compensation for doctors. It is accepted that when the majority of doctors in a given province have accepted the settlement of that province, that is what that concept means. The same applies to funding by hospitals. However, I will look into it and come back to my colleagues in Parliament with possible changes and more neutral words to try to define these two key concepts. We need concepts which are yardsticks of measurement for overcharges. Something has to be charged before we can define extra billing for user fees over and above the basis. By definition the basis must be serious enough not to create in itself an automatic way of creating user fees and extra billing.
So much for the text of the Bill itself in terms of possible legal changes to the Bill. The Bill is quite a short piece of legislation proposed for adoption by the House of Commons. I hope it will be adopted as soon as possible and that the Act will be in place by April 1. The Act does not do many new things. It basically consolidates the five existing conditions of

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
our medicare which have existed for 25 years for hospitals and 15 years for visits to doctors. It clarifies that two newer, growing problems, extra charges by doctors and specialists and user fees by provinces, contravene the Act. Because of that the federal Government will be deducting a dollar for a dollar. In a nutshell that is what the Act does.
It also has one other good input into medicare, which is a national institution, a beautiful and very important one: it introduces a process of resolution of problems which does not exist in the existing legislation. It is very good to put medicare above partisanship of all sorts. It is the biggest and most crucial institution for the citizens of a given country. Health is so precious. We are so well equipped in Canada and we want to reinforce and keep our medicare system. We are therefore also offering a process for the resolution of future problems with medicare. In other words, when there are extra charges a dollar for a dollar will be deducted. That is what is called the automatic penalty of the new Act.
There will be other breaches which cannot be anticipated. An example of this would be if hospitals were to be privatized and operated for profit in the private sector, which is against the spirit of our national programs which are publicly operated for non-profit for the benefit of all Canadians. When such future breaches develop there is a process offered by which Ministers, both federal and provincial, will have to exchange information by law. They will then have eventually to come to the federal Cabinet for an Order in Council defining what the penalty applicable to that particular breach is. The penalty does not have to be the whole cash contribution. That is a very disruptive penalty. The penalty might be anything judged by Cabinet at that time as appropriate to deter province x, y, or z from that breach. Within 15 days following that decision by the federal Cabinet the decision will have to be tabled here in the House of Commons and in the Senate. That is done to make sure it is brought into the open and before the public so that all regions of Canada have a fair chance to assess what the breach is and what the penalty is that is decided for that province.
By defining in our Bill the rules of the game as clearly and precisely as possible today we will avoid problems in the future and will have the best possible federal-provincial relations. This is the key in a system such as the medicare system.
[ Translation]
I have so much to say, and there is a great deal to say about the health insurance system. At this point, I would like to consider various aspects of health insurance which cannot be ignored and I would like to do so in connection with the political impact of Bill C-3 which has been felt across this country.

That does not stem from my visits last week to all the provinces in Canada. It is rooted in lots of experiences in the past month. I will first explain to everyone who is listening and to those who are with us in the House that it is very dangerous and bad for the social fabric of this big country of ours which
has so many diverse regions to believe, or to write, or to spread the word that, for example, this is an attack on Alberta. Nothing is farther from the truth and more dangerous and unfair for Albertans and all other Canadians.
By the way, that was written. Things like that feed opposition and lack of understanding instead of comprehension and bridges between the various regions of this huge country of ours. It does not stand the test of facts, figures and reality. That is why I have insisted that these twisted perceptions should be corrected.
For example, I received a form from a woman from Toronto approximately three or four days ago. It was from the Mount Sinai Hospital. There are many such forms charging extra billing for Canadian women who are perhaps 59 years of age. Many of these women are widows who are not entitled to their pension and who although not poor do not have enough money. In this particular case this form was submitted to the woman after the fact-which is wrong-and she was charged approximately $135. This was not even a personalized typewritten form but one which simply explained that her test in the general field of gynaecology was very specialized and concerned new technology. This woman is like millions of Canadian women who cannot judge. There are similar cases pertaining to men and children in the country with respect to sophisticated tests. Since OHIP only reimbursed her so much, she was asked to pay the extra amount of $135. I was told by medical officials that there was nothing new about these tests and therefore this woman, as a consumer, had already paid for them.
Perhaps cases such as this could be referred to my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola), who is also responsible for the status of women. This represents a double injustice because people are not protected from being asked to pay extra on top of what they have already paid. This example reflects hundreds of thousands of cases which have not been revealed and explains the grim realities of extra billing of at least some $50 million in Ontario and smaller amounts in most of the other provinces of Canada.
There are other examples of extra charges for admission, even to emergency, which is unbelievable when one considers it. Alberta is a particular case which has the potential of high user fees that have fortunately not yet been implemented by hospitals in that province, except for admission and other fees.
This brings me to another aspect of medicare. I do not know what the opinion of my colleagues is on this, but in the draft regulations which have been made available to my colleagues in the provinces last week and which we began discussing, we offered the concept that whenever there is a case of medical necessity people should not have to pay extra charges. While that is the view of this Government, some provinces have suggested that beyond 90 days or 120 days people will be charged daily. Another suggestion has been that one should pay every day in a particular kind of institution and not pay
January 16, 1984

when one is in another kind of bed. We do not believe that is good.
In this respect, I would say that each province can serve as a model in health care for a particular program, procedure or approach. In this case, Ontario is a model. There are many examples one can see in each of the ten provinces, and in this case Ontario has not practised a model of medical necessity.
When a patient has a potential of being reintegrated into the home, that patient should not be overcharged. I believe that makes sense. We do not often have a chance to discuss such things as medicare, which is so close to daily life, and I appreciate the opportunity. These are not concepts or theories but facts of life. We believe that if a person must pay for an apartment or pay a mortgage on a home, that person should not pay an overcharge.

This is the concept of medical need which we have put forward with regulations. It means for instance that, in the case of senior citizens who are living in old people's homes, these institutions are considered as their home. This is quite normal.
I do not believe that anyone will dispute that point; it is normal that these people use part of their pension to pay a daily amount for food and maintenance as well as for accommodation cost, if I may use such a term.
It is very important to say so. However, in the case of someone of whatever age who is in a chronic care bed for perhaps four, five or six months, such as those who have suffered serious burns which take much longer to heal, and who, whatever his age will be able to resume a normal life, such an individual must also keep his home or his apartment. He has double costs. He is therefore a patient and has no business paying any surcharge. This is the definition that we give in the regulations. Needless to say that this was one case where the provinces tried to take advantage of the system, and the reaction to this has been quite strong-

I would like parliamentarians to pay great attention to that because we are fixing the rules of the game of medicare for years to come. I would not wish any Minister of Health to go through it again. We want to consolidate medicare by fixing the loopholes and bad habits that have developed to make it work for years to come.
My colleague, the Minister from Alberta, said at the conclusion of our meetings last week that he was very surprised to see that admission to emergency and other admissions were not acceptable overcharges. We do not believe they are acceptable because they stand in the way of health care in an emergency situation as well as the fact that Canadians have already paid for such an event. While I would not say it is a right, they have prepaid this through their taxes and we owe it to them. This is what the federal Government pays for with over $9 billion. We are not interested in any other kind of system and we believe it is the best, most efficient and least expensive way to administer it compared to the United States.
Canada Health Act
For those reasons the proposals by that Alberta Minister for admission fees or user fees which exist in his province are unacceptable, and he is not the only Minister who suggested this. These charges are not acceptable for patients who have the potential for being medically reintegrated into normal daily life. The Minister was most surprised when I explained that those charges would not be acceptable, but he is new in the job. Officials from both sides, federal and provincial, remember the pre-block funding days of 1976 and before. During the entire period of the cost-sharing mechanism under which the system works and for which we had direct control, we deducted these charges.
Why do I not name Judy LaMarsh as one of the Ministers of Health who had to do that? She would sign payments to a province on which we had first deducted these extra charges. We had deducted a buck for a buck, a dollar for a dollar, already. We can go back 25 years and see the charges that were not authorized, that were not in the spirit of medicare, were always deducted. I do not think the officials will like what I am saying. Maybe we will have to use a computer to get that information out of the system to tell everybody how much it was. We always deducted a dollar for a dollar of any user charges that were applied to people who could be medically returned to normal life. We always did that and we want to continue doing that. That is the medicare we want. That is the way we want Canadians to be treated.
Why is it that we want Canadians to be treated like that? Some think we are socializing health, whatever that means, or turning our health services into a state medical system or whatever words are used these days. The reality is very clear. Canadians as a society, as a community, first 25 years ago and then in a second step 15 years ago decided to prepay everything that has to do with going to the hospital on the one hand and with going to the doctor on the other. In other words, we gave ourselves as a community, as a country, a program by which we pay ahead of time what is needed to have medicare. We want to keep it that way. The fiction, because it is absolute fiction, is that some believe that premiums, which are a very different way of paying for health care, cost far less than paying by general taxes. They must have been really bad in arithmetic when they were kids at school.
Let us review what that means. First, a Canadian who lives in one of the three provinces which levy premiums has already paid for medicare through taxes, provincial taxes of the province, and then a tiny portion of the whole medicare cost of that province comes to the province through premiums. The problem with premiums is that they hit people in a very unfair way. They hit poor people in exactly the same way as those with lots of money. To my way of thinking, that is totally wrong.
Second, premiums cost a lot of money administratively. A special mechanism has to be set up to collect premiums. Then, how does one enforce their collection? It is none of my business but I told some of my provincial colleagues that there is nothing which prevents them from having on the tax form,

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
which we the federal Government administer on their behalf, a special part to tell us what they want to show separately as going to medicare. They think premiums are a good way to remind Canadians of the real cost of health. They are not. Premiums are too high and create a problem for some who do not have money, but they are far too low to show the real cost of health.
Maybe the tax form is the better mechanism to use. It would be very easy. Maybe the whole amount of the premiums should be converted into tax points and then people would pay according to their means, which is the progressive way for any modern society to obtain and develop programs.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That would ensure that no one is denied services because of unpaid premiums. Everybody should pay their share, there is no doubt about that, but that share should be separate and apart from getting the health service you need when you need it. What about someone who has not paid his tax? My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), does his job and he does it very well. He makes sure everybody pays their taxes as everybody is supposed to.
Sure, whether they owe them or not. You are harbingers of doom.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Everybody should pay their taxes. I am very pleased to see the Conservatives agree with that. I was myself Minister of National Revenue and I know taxes are the basis for any programs to be developed. But if the tax collector gets after those how have not paid their taxes, that has nothing to do with medicare. He or she should do his or her job and get his or her taxes paid. That is absolutely normal in any society. But that has nothing to do with getting health services in a doctor's office or in a hospital when a person needs it. That is why I say premiums are quite a fiction. Many things are a fiction.
You mean they do not exist?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I think on the first page of The Toronto Star on Friday morning it was reported that the new Canada Health Act will impose a $500 million expenditure on Ontario. That is absolute fiction. Right now Ontario does not have much in the way of user fees to my knowledge. Ontario has about $50 million in extra billing. The new Act, until the situation returns to normal, will impose a penalty of $50 million. Why multiply that figure and make it $500 million? Is that an admission by the Province of Ontario that it has not paid its doctors enough in the past? No, I cannot believe that would be the way things would go.
Do not speculate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Let us talk of facts. I am sure the Member does not know them.
There has been a 36 per cent increase in British Columbia. Do you want that to happen in Ontario?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The Hon. Member does not seem to realize that extra billing has nothing to do with an increase of budget and of cost in any given province. To answer the Hon. Member, the vast majority are, yes. The vast majority of doctors in the health system do not extra bill. Doctor x gets extra bucks for himself or herself from the system, which amounts in some parts of the country to hundreds of thousands of dollars for one person. Why is that? Is that person better than the doctor next door? I say prove it. Nobody can prove something like that.
You are dangerous.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Having good management and good procedures in the health system have nothing to do with permitting extra billing or creating user fees supposedly to deter Canadians from abusing the system. Canadians are not abusers of the health system.

Nobody likes to wait for hours in an out-patient department or the emergency department, nobody. Try it if you need to be convinced. This is what medicare is all about.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, January 11, 1984, my office received a news release dated December 21, 1983, from the Hon. Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia). This news release informed me of his Department's new initiative in conservation and job creation, called "Environment 2000".
The stated deadline for receipt of completed applications at the nearest Environment Canada regional office-in the case of my riding, Edmonton, Alberta-was the end of January. However, as of January 11 blank application forms were unavailable at the Edmonton office. While the existence of such a project is of real interest to a riding such as my own, Dauphin-Swan River, the time frame given both to myself and to those of my constituents who may wish to act upon Environment 2000 is absolutely ridiculous.
When I contacted the local Ottawa Environment Canada office to ask for an explanation of the above, the response was less than adequate. I am now told that the application deadline has been extended until February 15, 1984. This revised February 15, 1984, deadline still does not provide sufficient time for prospective applicants in my riding to be informed of the project, obtain application forms from Edmonton, formulate their proposals, complete the necessary paperwork, and return the materials to Edmonton.
My constituents and I would like to know how seriously the Environment Minister wants to see our riding's unemployed young people benefit from Environment 2000. We would suggest that he take the necessary steps-
1 regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the hiring restrictions placed on the selection of workers for job-creation projects in Canada funded directly by provincial Governments and the Canada Works Program funded directly by the federal Government, are an example of blatant, outright discrimination in hiring practices.
The criteria respecting who qualifies for work on provincially and federally sponsored works programs were designed for urban areas. Over the past two weeks referrals have been going out from Manpower Offices in Canada for Canada Works projects with preferences given to exhaustees and welfare recipients. Persons with no income, or new entrants into the work force, cannot even obtain a referral because of these departmental restrictions. Instead of leaving selection to sponsoring groups in the community, Canada Manpower is forced by these regulations to omit those without any income.
These regulations came into force during the NEED Program upon request of provincial Governments that made deals with the federal Government. I am requesting the Minister responsible to intervene immediately to throw these restrictions out the window. The Opposition should be making an issue of it.
Hear, hear!

POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER BY UNITED STATES CHEMICAL DUMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) and his predecessor have both called the S-area dump on the United States side of the Niagara River "a greater threat to Canadian waters than any other U.S. landfill uncovered to date". The Minister has indicated that the clean up of this S-area site will be a priority issue in talks with his American counterparts, and in his Department.
This dump is a seven-acre site, about 300 feet from the Niagara River. An estimated 63,000 tons of chemicals are buried in it. Just recently an Environment Canada report claimed that some of these chemicals are finding their way into the Niagara River.
A settlement has now been reached between Hooker Chemicals and the State of New York, by which the company is required to take whatever steps are deemed technically and economically feasible by the United States court. Unlike the Hyde Park settlement when witnesses were allowed to present evidence in court before the court approved the settlement, this time Canadians and Americans will be allowed only 30 days for comment before approval is given. The nature of the settlement document and the problem itself are too technical and intricate for environmental agencies to comment upon within that time period. An intervention by the Government of Canada before the public comment period has expired is urgent and necessary so as to protect Canadian public interest.

subtopic: REFUSAL OF SERVICE TO OTTAWA APARTMENT BUILDING
REFUSAL OF SERVICE TO OTTAWA APARTMENT BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Ottawa we hear that mail service is being refused to a new apartment building housing 200 families because of a shortage of carriers. This is ridiculous. Not only does Canada Post service a building right across the street, but there are 18 positions in the bureaucracy in Ottawa paying in excess of $50,000, all the way to a staggering $227,000.
Surely a way can be found to deliver mail to an apartment building which might take an hour per day to handle. At the same time, perhaps one of them could hop on the stagecoach to Fort Erie and discover why a letter containing important cheques from the social security service in Buffalo takes two weeks to travel across the river to Fort Erie. Why, in the name of all reason and logic, must mail for the Niagara area go to Toronto to be sorted? Someone in the hierarchy needs to take lessons in common sense. Imagine the wasted time, gasoline and manpower, especially when Canada Post has decided to be financially cautious. If it really wants to be financially cautious, there is only one route to go-cut out the deadwood in the bureaucracy and make more efficient use of the work force already available. Then, and only then, will there be a chance that Canadians will be satisfied with their postal service.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am concerned at the language of deception that is currently used in describing the act of abortion. This vocabulary is used in such a way as to falsify and pervert the true meaning of the Act. For example, instead of saying or admitting that abortion kills a baby, or fetus, or embryo, it is said that a pregnancy was "terminated". Similarly, the operative procedure of abortion is listed as "therapeutic". However the term therapeutic means to cure or to heal. So-called therapeutic abortion satisfies no therapeutic criteria. It treats no disease, cures no symptoms, and does not remove, in the vast majority of cases, abnormal tissues.
Herbert Spencer, in his book entitled Principles of Ethics, said, "How often misused words generate misleading thoughts". I can think of no better example of misuse of words than the current usage of language in the social sciences through the use of misleading soft terms, such as "therapeutic abortion" and "termination of pregnancy", to obscure the full meaning and full impact of abortion.

subtopic: CONTAMINATED WATER SPILLS AT KEY LAKE URANIUM MINE, SASK.
CONTAMINATED WATER SPILLS AT KEY LAKE URANIUM MINE, SASK.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 5 over 100 million litres of radium 226 contaminated water spilled at the Key Lake uranium mine in northern Saskatchewan. There is no doubt that a serious threat exists to the environment and the health and safety of northern residents and workers. Left in the environment, radium 226 will spread through the Athabasca and Churchill Rivers systems. It will be digested by fish which are eaten by people.
This is not the only spill. There have been 15 others, nine with radioactive material, in the last six months. So far we have been lucky. Had the spill occurred at the Rabbit Lake mine, it would have flowed straight into Collins Bay, making it impossible to clean up. Had the spill occurred in the summer, or had it gone into sand rather than the muskeg, it would have flowed straight into the water table.
Serious technical problems exist. Unfortunately, they are compounded by mindless provincial government decisions. The Saskatchewan Conservative Government is hell bent on development, deregulation, and government cutbacks. It reduced by 40 per cent the number of people monitoring the uranium mines. It ignored the lease agreement which provided for a monitoring committee to meet at the mine site three times a year. It wants the revenue from the mines, but is negligent in its concern for northern residents, the workers, and the environment.
In the name of sanity and for generations yet to come, let us preserve the North. Stop the uranium mining.

It is my understanding that the spills that have happened at the mine site, some 15 in total since the beginning of its operation, are to be reported to Saskatchewan Environment. subsubtopic: "THE INVESTIGATIVE APPROACH TO AUDITING"-REQUEST FOR SCREENING OF TRAINING FILM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. The Minister will know from his Liberal colleagues that the conduct of his Department is now at the top of the list of grievances received by Members of Parliament from people across Canada. I think this stems from the obvious policy of the Department to encourage aggressive tax collection techniques-techniques that are symbolized in the training film entitled The Investigative Approach to Auditing.
Is the Minister prepared to have a showing of this training film for interested Members of Parliament and members of the press this week, so that we will have an idea of the kind of incentives being put before the auditors in his Department?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: "THE INVESTIGATIVE APPROACH TO AUDITING"-REQUEST FOR SCREENING OF TRAINING FILM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about this charge of aggressivity about the way the Department collects taxes. I am also concerned about another problem. I would like to quote Hon. Members a few figures. For instance, in 1982-83, the Department was responsible for the collection of about $2.6 billion in
taxes due, that is taxes that must be collected if we want to guarantee an equitable system. At the end of the first eight months of 1983-84, there is an amount of $3.5 billion of receivable accounts or taxes due. This question should concern all the members of this House since these are taxes due.
As for the film used to train certain departmental employees, I have already told the House that if members of the Standing Committee responsible for consideration of these matters were interested in looking at it and discussing its contents, its objectives, and its use by departmental officials, I would be happy to organize a meeting with our officials, who will readily answer the various questions which may be asked.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is shrouding his Department in oppressive secrecy. Employees of the Minister's Department have reported that Revenue Canada has been cooking the books in its favour when a taxpayer fails to make a deduction to which he or she is entitled. There is no other word for this except "cheating". Will the Minister, therefore, do the honourable thing and make a commitment to every taxpayer in this country that the Department will stop cheating Canadians by dressing tax returns and, instead, correct those returns to the taxpayer's benefit?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again I want all Canadian taxpayers to know that we make every effort to examine tax returns objectively. For instance, in the routine examination of tax returns, we save taxpayers thousands of dollars by making a first examination of their returns. Our objective is not to collect more taxes. Our objective at the Department of National Revenue is to guarantee that every Canadian taxpayer pays his own share of taxes, no more, no less!

subtopic: DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES
DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. A constituent of mine, Mr. David Bourne, has felt the sting of the Income Tax Act. He has been denied the deduction for expenses related to the cost of leg braces and is being told by National Revenue officials that he should use a wheelchair. He does not want a wheelchair. He is more mobile with leg braces. Noting that the Tax Appeal Board has upheld the appeal of Mr. Michael Overdyk whose disability is similar to Mr. Bourne's, will the Minister instruct his officials to treat the Overdyk ruling as a precedent and apply it to Mr. Bourne and others with disabilities which affect their mobility and ability to earn an income?
January 16, 1984

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: DENIAL OF DEDUCTION FOR LEG BRACES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad the Hon. Member raised this question. He is referring to the judgement in a specific court case, the Overdyk case. First of all, I would like to assure the Hon. Member, that the Department will not appeal that decision. The Department accepts as rendered the decision in the Overdyk case, and I would simply assure the Hon. Member, other Members in the House and the Canadian taxpayers that anyone involved in a situation similar to the one examined by the Court in the Overdyk case will be treated the same way.
However, I cannot tell him that the case he is referring to is similar, that the circumstances are the same as in the Overdyk case. The Hon. Member should bear in mind that the decision in that case was based on specific facts, and that other cases that are to be considered in the light of that decision should meet the criteria of specific circumstances as examined by the Court in the Overdyk case.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. A committee of this House on disabled and handicapped persons recommended that the Income Tax Act be amended so that allowances for expenses incurred by disabled persons who are employed and earning be classed as deductible expenses for tax purposes. Will the Minister show some initiative and get a commitment from the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare to define the term "disability" more broadly, and accept recommendation No. 46 of the special committee, so that cases such as David Bourne and Professor Nagler of Hamilton, who is disabled with cerebral palsy, will be covered?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Hon. Member is raising the issue in a much broader context, that of taxation policy in respect of the handicapped.
We on the Government side are privileged in having within our ranks a colleague, the present Minister of State (Small Businesses), who has chaired a committee of this House, and has together with other Members made us much aware of the problems of the handicapped in general and of their problems with respect to the Income Tax Act. And I must add that this has enabled me to identify certain situations in which the handicapped are deprived of the very restrictive provision now found in the Income Tax Act, and I can assure the Hon. Member that I will bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance those specific cases in order that, when the time comes for him to make policy decisions concerning amendments to the Income Tax Act, he will consider whether it is possible
Oral Questions
within the spirit of the existing Act to bring forward whatever amendments would implement such proposals.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. A number of Ministers have talked in recent days about the recovery which took place in 1983. However, according to statistics released by government Departments and agencies themselves in the past week, it is clear that the recovery has been anything but fair. For example, while profit increases of corporations almost doubled, going up by 96 per cent in 1983 as compared to 1982, instead of going down average unemployment levels increased by about a full percentage point. Why should the Prime Minister expect Canada in 1984 will have any fairer kind of recovery by maintaining the same policies, which include tax increases on consumers and tax reductions for corporations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must have misunderstood the Hon. Member. I understood him to say that unemployment had gone up. In 1983, from December to December, it had fallen from 12.8 per cent to 11.1 per cent or 11.2 per cent. It is true that profits have gone up. The Minister of Finance has commented on that on various occasions. I believe he indicated that they have gone up. They have not recovered the position which they had before the economic downturn.
Of course, in our system, profits are important. It is with profits that investments are made and that jobs are created. Therefore, we do not feel distressed that profits have gone up. We do hope that they will result in greater creation of jobs.
Once again, as the Minister of Finance has indicated, and he has quoted figures, there has been very substantial job creation in the last 12 months, bringing unemployment down by a full point and three quarters.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister should read his own Government's reports. The average unemployment for the year in fact went up. More seriously, what is indicated for 1984, according to private and government forecasting agencies, is that the profits which are now being made are not being reinvested to create the jobs about which the Prime Minister is talking.
Considering that forecasters are saying that unemployment in 1984 is going to remain above 11 per cent, which is a way beyond the pre-1981 recession level, but profits are going to go up beyond the 1981 profit level, will the Prime Minister not admit that this is an unfair kind of recovery? And will the Government bring in some immediate programs which will start to produce the jobs which unemployed Canadians want?

January 16, 1984
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the admission which the Leader of the New Democratic Party is seeking leads me to think that the only thing which I can admit is that the New Democratic Party is, true to form, looking back on 1983, which has been a year of growth, where inflation has fallen, where jobs were created at an unexpected rate. Naturally, looking back on the year, the Hon. Member still does not think it is good enough. Looking ahead to the times to come, he is still hypothesizing that it will be a very bad year. That is typical of the New Democratic Party. There has been surprising progress in 1983. It has to continue, and it will not continue with the defeatist spirit shown by the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister will not pay attention to the questions, perhaps he will read his own Government's reports. I am not talking about what the New Democratic Party has said about 1984, but about what government agencies have said about 1984.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CHANGE CORPORATION TAX POLICY
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CHANGE CORPORATION TAX POLICY
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
Prime Minister again specifically, since the proposal made by his Minister of Finance to the effect that we should give all kinds of blanket tax concessions to the corporations, which will in turn invest this money and create jobs, has evidently not worked, will the Government now change its policy and tie any tax cuts to the corporations to specific performance, either in terms of R and D or in terms of job creation? That is one change which the Government could make.
Would the Government also rescind the more than one billion dollar tax increases which are scheduled to go into effect for consumers? In short, will the Government reverse some of its policies in order to produce the jobs which Canadians want?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT CHANGE CORPORATION TAX POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 hope that the New Democratic Party will reverse some of its stands as well. I have in mind that in the November, 1982, Budget we proposed closing a great number of loopholes which were advantageous to corporations and higher income earners. As Mr. Laxer points out, the New Democratic Party there again preferred pious phrases and did not support the Government in a very progressive series of budget measures. If the Hon. Member is counselling reversal of policies, he had better begin looking at his own record.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF OFFICIAL'S REPORTED STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National
Revenue. We have been subjected for some days in this House to charges and counter charges with regard to the application of the Income Tax Act. Today the Member for Cambridge has purportedly quoted an official of the Department of Revenue as contradicting the Minister. In order to allay the suspicions of the public, will the Minister cause an investigation to be carried out to determine whether or not those charges were actually made by that official in violation of the statement made here by the Minister and, if so, when will that official be disciplined?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF OFFICIAL'S REPORTED STATEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF OFFICIAL'S REPORTED STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know very well the Hon. Member who asked this question, and I would urge him not to be influenced by such insidious accusations, and especially by the totally erroneous conclusions drawn by Opposition Members from statements made by people who do not even have the guts to identify themselves.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue. It concerns the taxation of farmers. The Minister must realize that many farmers have had to take off-farm jobs in these difficult times. Revenue Canada has been aggressively auditing these people and in many cases has reclassified them, either as part time or hobby farmers, and disallowed all or part of their farm losses. Paul E. Graham, of Lambton County in Ontario, is one such victim, having been reassessed $18,000. In October Mr. Graham had this decision reversed by the Federal Court of Canada. However, Revenue Canada has now appealed the case.
In light of the fact that there are so many farmers in the same position as Mr. Graham, will the Minister not call off his auditors and stop the harassment by the collection department until this unfair issue is clearly settled?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will remind the Hon. Member that the provisions of the Income Tax Act concerning farmers are very specific. He knows how the classifications are drawn up and what privileges are enjoyed by each. I would also remind the Hon. Member that there is in the Income Tax Act a provision whereby the Minister must collect taxes, from the moment such taxes are assessed or a notification of assessment is issued, even in instances where the taxpayer appeals his notification of assessment as to its amount or its nature. I would remind the Hon. Member that this is a clear responsibility given the Minister by the Income Tax Act. Therefore, I cannot meet the Hon. Member's request to ignore the assessment
January 16, 1984

notifications that were issued under the provisions of the Income Tax Act in respect of those taxpayers, because the Income Tax Act is clear. It lays upon the Minister of Revenue the obligation of collecting those taxes. If the Hon. Member wants the Department officials and the Minister to ignore the Income Tax Act, as is apparently the wish of some of his colleagues, he should say so clearly, rather than implying that there is at that level liberty or discretion to do otherwise.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER STOP COURT ACTION
REQUEST THAT MINISTER STOP COURT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Minister would take the time to read the federal cases he would see that every judge has commented on how ambiguous, unfair, unclear and poorly worded is this legislation. It is not precise at all. Why does the Minister not simply call off the Department and have his officials drop the case against Graham, and stop harassing farmers who are such an important part of our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER STOP COURT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has referred to the court decision in that specific case. I would remind him that within my Department, as I have already pointed out to him before Christmas, a close review of the nature of the Court decision was made. After that review, we held discussions with representatives of the Department of Justice, and we reached the same conclusion that in view of the implications of the provisions of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act, it was the Minister's duty to appeal the judge's decision. We are waiting for the higher court to study the case and render its decision, before having a further examination of the issue.
In the meantime, we will go on administering the Act as it is.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF ARTISTS AND WRITERS
DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF ARTISTS AND WRITERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Revenue. On November 2, by a unanimous decision of this House, it was required that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture deal as a top priority with the question of taxing artists and writers in Canada. Since that time, two and one half months ago, the Committee has not met, no action has been taken, and the Minister has failed to stop the tax persecutions of these people. Much damage has been done.
Hundreds of artists are now echoing the comments made by David Silverberg, Professor of Fine Arts at Mount Allison University, an internationally known artist. He said: "Canadian artists are demoralized, dejected, and even stupified by the onslaught from Revenue Canada". Will the Minister not ask his colleagues to proceed with that Committee now? More important, will the Minister not put a hold on those taxes and
Oral Questions
tax assessments which are so unjust and unfair to those people?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF ARTISTS AND WRITERS
speechtext: Just as all the other Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, surely you must be aware that I am not responsible for the operation of the various committees. Committee members must decide on their own when they are to meet and what they will deal with. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, there is no provision in the Income Tax Act which would make it possible for the Minister of National Revenue to exempt certain groups of taxpayers from paying income tax. As a matter of fact, the Minister of National Revenue must make sure that these groups pay taxes on their income. If the Hon. Member feels that changes should be made or that a special status should exist under the Income Tax Act for artists and writers, he should make concrete proposals to the committee or the Minister of Finance, and if the Minister of Finance happened to share his views, he would introduce a bill to amend the Income Tax Act which the House would eventually have to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, over the last four months I have tried to deal fairly and honestly with this Minister, but my patience is at an end. The Minister must know the absurdity. If Van Gogh or any other great artist were living in this country today as a Canadian citizen, he would not be assessed by the Minister's Department as an artist; he would be assessed as a hobbyist or a failed manufacturer.
The Minister is responsible, not the officials. If the Minister will not put a hold on, and will not do anything to help, will he at least instruct his officials to use the definition which has already been adopted by the United Nations, in the interim, so that these people can have some sense of equity about taxation in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just witnessed a great performance by an artist, an actor, a sort of Tartuffe. That is someone who knows something and who feigns ignorance.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would like me to give my officials the authority to decide what will be in the Income Tax Act. What I want, personally, is that the government introduce legislation and that the House preserve its right to amend the Income Tax Act. Period.

January 16, 1984

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF ACT
speechtext: I regret that the Leader of the Opposition did not seek more information from his advisors before asking such a question. Is the Minister telling us that there is nothing he can do, that he is only the messenger of the Minister of Finance? He has responsibilities towards the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: HONG KONG-SUGGESTED MEDIATION ROLE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Considering that many of the over 200,000 Canadians of Chinese background have relatives in Hong Kong, will the Prime Minister raise in his meetings tomorrow with the Chinese Premier, Zhao Ziyang, Canadian interest in the early settlement of the Hong Kong issue between Britain and China? Considering that Canada is a former British colony and we have solved some of the legal problems that Hong Kong will have to face and solve, and considering that the Prime Minister's policy has been quite progressive toward China over the years, does he see a mediation role for Canada in the settlement of the Hong Kong issue between Britain and China?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: HONG KONG-SUGGESTED MEDIATION ROLE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question does interest Canada but only in an indirect way. We have many Canadian interests which deal with Hong Kong and trade with Hong Kong. Naturally we are interested in the future of that Crown colony. It is possible that we will discuss the subject.
I must add that I do not see the Canadian Government playing what the Hon. Member describes as an intermediary role. I think we will be interested in ensuring that what happens in Hong Kong is conducive to more successful economic trading with Hong Kong by Canadians, and is a path which is acceptable both to the citizens of Hong Kong and to the two major powers involved.
January 16, 1984

subsubtopic: RIGHT OF ONTARIO STUDENTS TO EDUCATION IN FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice. Has he been made aware that the Michipicoten Board of Education, located in the northern Ontario town of Wawa, has passed a resolution which will have the effect of excluding 60 French speaking students from attending high school in the fall of this year? These 60 students come from the community of Dubreuilville, located in my constituency. The Board is having a dispute with the Government of Ontario regarding francophone representation on boards of education, and these students are being used as pawns. Would the Minister of Justice tell us how the constitutional rights of these young people may be protected, the right to an education in their language and the right to attend school and facilities that are in reasonable proximity to them, and to have these paid for out of public funds?
Privilege-Mr. Beatty

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF ONTARIO STUDENTS TO EDUCATION IN FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I thank the Hon. Member for bringing this situation to my attention. The Secretary of State has a program under which, on the advice of the Minister of Justice, he extends funding in appropriate places to challenges based on language under the new Constitution.
As my hon. friend will know, the Province of Ontario is not subject to the provisions of Sections 16 to 22 dealing with official languages under the Charter. From the situation I understand my hon. friend to pose, this does involve a minority language education problem and it could possibly be dealt with under the provisions of the Sections of the Charter beginning with Section 23.
There is, I believe, this week being argued in the Ontario Court of Appeal a reference, with my Department as an intervenor, in which the Ontario Government has asked the Ontario Court of Appeal to establish what the rights are with respect to language and minority education in the Province of Ontario. I would hope that case will be decided well before the beginning of the new academic term and that it will provide the kind of clarification necessary to protect the rights of these students. Failing that, of course, they can always bring an action on their own behalf, perhaps with the assistance of the Secretary of State's funding.
