MR. BEATTY-ALLEGED FALSE STATEMENT OF MR. BUSSIt-RES

Mr. Speaker, the rules of the House require me to raise a question of privilege at the earliest possible opportunity. During Question Period today I gave you notice of my intention to raise a question of privilege if the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) deliberately allowed to stand on the record a false statement which he had made, I assume in error, on December 21, 1983.

Privilege-Mr. Beatty
I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, page 395 of Hansard. It reads in part:

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. On November 29 last I challenged the Minister on the existence of quotas for auditors in the city of Kitchener. At that time he denied quotas in fact existed. He recanted on Monday, saying quotas did exist but that he had issued a directive to stop them. He assured the House, and gave us his undertaking, that quotas did not exist anywhere else in Canada. In the two days since last Monday has the Minister had time to reflect on whether or not quotas still exist? Will he give us an undertaking today that there are no quotas for auditors in Canada?

With all due respect to the Hon. Member, he has given notice of this matter as privilege. The Chair is actively considering the matter which was put before the House as privilege. It appears to be a matter relating to the Minister of National Revenue?
It is a distinct question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe.

Mr. Speaker, I will establish that this is a separate and distinct question of privilege, a separate offence against the privileges of Members of this House.
The response given by the Minister of National Revenue on December 21, 1983 is as follows:
Madam Speaker, as I have indicated to the House before, it is not departmental policy to set quotas for amounts to be assessed by auditors of the Department of National Revenue. As I have also had occasion to inform the House, an unfortunate initiative-
And this is the central phrase, "the only one of its kind", clearly referring to the Kitchener case which was the only one being raised in Parliament to that date.
-was taken in a district office, and as soon as it was brought to the attention of senior departmental officials, the latter asked the person who took the initiative to stop this procedure immediately, and this was even before the Hon. Member had an opportunity to raise the issue in the House, that is to say, at the time the Hon. Member brought up the subject, this isolated initiative had been stopped. Madam Speaker, I have received the assurance of senior departmental officials that our policy not to have such quotas is observed across Canada.
Later that same day I did indeed raise a question of privilege with Madam Speaker with regard to the Minister's statements as they related to Kitchener. I pointed out at that time that the Minister had made statements with regard to Kitchener when he had been asked by Members on this side of the House and had indicated that there were not quotas in place with regard to the Kitchener office. I will not go over the grounds that I covered at that time. I believe I gave substantial grounds for a question of privilege. The response, Mr. Speaker, was not given by the Minister. The Minister did not deign to enter into the discussion that day. The response was given by a Parliamentary Secretary.
The Chair is well aware of the incident cited by the Hon. Member. Could the Hon. Member get to his separate question of privilege?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Allow him to do so.

Mr. Speaker, what I am trying to do is establish why this is different. This is different on two grounds. First, it is a separate instance. The Minister today took the action having had pointed out to him false information which he had put on the record which had not been pointed out to him previously. The Minister chose to leave that false information intact on the record, and I will get back to that point in a minute.
Second, the defence that was offered, not by the Minister but by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans), in the Kitchener incident is not applicable today. The defence offered was that the Minister unknowingly told the truth in the case of Kitchener, but the Minister, without knowing in fact what had taken place, said that quotas did not exist in Kitchener at that time and that, in fact, his officials, without his knowing it, had indeed cancelled the quotas in Kitchener.
That was the argument made in that instance. That question of privilege stands on its own and you are considering it at the present time. What I am asking you to look at today is the statement with regard to Toronto made on December 21, where the Minister stated explicitly that there was only one instance, one isolated instance in Canada, where quotas have been put in place in a district office, and that was it-clearly referring strictly to Kitchener.
On that same day my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), produced documentation proving that there were quotas in place in Toronto. The Minister has had since December 21 to examine the statement that he put on the record that day and to get back to the House and correct it. On at least four separate occasions this afternoon in Question Period, the Minister was asked specifically with regard to that statement-not with regard to Kitchener but with regard to that statement-made on December 21. He was asked whether he would correct the record or whether he would allow the falsehood to stand.
The Minister has in his hand further documentation which was produced to him by the Hon. Member for Cambridge this afternoon. This further documentary evidence proves beyond a shadow of a doubt that quotas existed in Kitchener. The Minister knows it. The documentation is in his hands. He knows what the truth is.
Additionally, Mr. Speaker, during Question Period today, unless the Minister claim ignorance, he had quoted to him the statement made publicly with identification by the director of the Toronto district taxation office who said expressly that quotas had existed in Toronto. This statement was printed in the Toronto Globe and Mail of last Saturday. The Minister would have been aware of that statement. It was included in the departmental clippings summary this morning which he will have received. That statement was quoted during Question Period to the Minister. It was alluded to, I gather, by the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), who made reference to it as well. The Minister cannot today claim ignorance.
January 16, 1984

What are the options, Mr. Speaker? First, the director of the Toronto district tax office lied to The Globe and Mail, or in addition the documentation in the Minister's hands now was forged in some way, that it is not in fact what it appears to be. That is direct proof of the existence of quotas in Toronto. Second, an error took place in this documentation and the director was misquoted by The Globe and Mail, yet there has been no indication either on the part of the Minister or on the part of the director, as we have seen today, that any attempt has been made to get The Globe and Mail to rescind the direct statement made by the director of the Toronto district taxation office that quotas had existed. The third possibility is that The Globe and Mail and the documentation produced today are absolutely accurate and that indeed quotas did exist and were in place when the Minister was denying that such a thing had taken place in any place but Kitchener.
Mistakes are made daily in the House of Commons. Each of us has had occasion to say something we later discovered was in error. Nobody would fault a Member for that. Nobody faults the Minister for that. If the Minister were to have responded today during Question Period and had told the House that he was in error when he made the statement that there was only one isolated incident in the country, namely in Kitchener, where quotas existed, and if he were to have said "Here are the facts; I correct that statement", there would have been no question of privilege.
The Minister, having had the falsehood pointed out to him and having been given the opportunity to correct the record, chose his words very carefully in response to allow that falsehood to stand on the record unchanged. Instead, he responded with regard to the broad policy of the Department, not as to whether district tax offices had quotas in place.
The point which you must consider, Mr. Speaker, in protecting the rights of all Members of Parliament, when a statement made in innocent ignorance at the time is proven to be false, when the person who made the statement knows that it is false and is given an opportunity to correct a false statement, as the Minister was on at least four or five separate incidents today, and when he deliberately chooses not to do that, is whether that is tantamount to deliberately leaving a false statement on the record of the House of Commons. If it is, there can be no difference between that and deliberately uttering a falsehood.
It would be absurd to say that it was against the rules of the House of Commons for a Member deliberately to mislead the House when he makes a statement and then to say that it is acceptable and somehow excusable, if he said something in ignorance, made no effort to correct it and left the false information on the record. They are part and parcel of the same thing. If the Minister is allowed to leave statements which he knows to be false on the record uncorrected, the privileges of all Hon. Members are in jeopardy.
If you find, Mr. Speaker, that I have a prima facie case of privilege, I would be prepared to move the appropriate motion.
Privilege-Mr. Beatty

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two things here that must be considered. First of all, we must look at the situation and the facts. We have the general administration of the Department of National Revenue located here in Ottawa, there are various district offices across Canada, which act according to a general policy set by Headquarters in Ottawa. A departmental policy is one that originates from the Directorate General at the Deputy Minister level here in Ottawa and is implemented in all district offices across Canada. I feel we must first understand what a departmental policy and its general practice is, before we go any further.
The second point we must consider: Did I, as the Hon. Member claims, intend to deceive the House when I answered his questions? The question was whether quotas had been set for auditors in the Department of National Revenue, concerning certain sums of money they were supposed to collect, and other matters. I made it clear that it was not the policy of the Department of National Revenue. When I was told about one situation, I made inquiries among senior officials in my Department, and in my answer to the House I stated again that it was not departmental policy, that I had been informed it was an isolated case, and that basically, the Department's policy was observed everywhere. I may remind the House that when a directive is not issued by the Deputy Minister here in Ottawa, it is not considered to be departmental policy.
Second, I pointed out earlier to the House that senior officials of my Department had given me the assurance that a policy not to have quotas was followed by the Department, and moreover, I asked for a directive to be prepared, and that is being done. That will ensure that any unfortunate initiatives that had existed or might exist would be immediately done away with. Mr. Speaker, this was clearly an indication of my concern that if the information I had was not complete, because in isolated cases initiatives could be taken, which is normal in such a large administration, that if such initiatives had been taken, contrary to department policy, we wanted to put a stop to such initiatives. Mr. Speaker, I don't think it was my intention to deceive the House, on the contrary, I wanted to give the House the assurance that the Department's policies were properly carried out across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief; I only wish to add an addendum to the comments of the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty). The point is that on November 29 I asked whether or not quotas existed in Kitchener. There was a denial. I believe the Minister to be an honourable man, and he denied any knowledge of the existence of those quotas. I have advised them that I personally trusted the Minister and took his word as being honest. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief and will not go over the arguments already presented by Hon. Members on this side who have contributed to the submission of privilege to date. I simply want to re-emphasize the practice in this place of proceeding on the basis of establishing a prima facie case of privilege. That is all that the Chair requires to have before it in order to trigger the process of dealing further with the matter.
I have before me, and I listened carefully as it was presented by the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), Hansard of December 21 where the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) is clearly on record as saying that the quota system which was part of the Kitchener operation was the only one of its kind that was taken in a district office and that, as soon as it was brought to the attention of senior departmental officials, the latter asked the person who took the initiative to stop this procedure immediately.
The important part of that evidence is the statement by the Minister that it was "the only one of its kind". A little further on on the same page, 395, he referred to the Kitchener quota system as being "this isolated initiative". Very dear evidence has been read into the record today and provided to the Minister from a departmental document entitled "Office Examination and Adjustments, Goals and Objectives, 198384". On page three of that document it is very clear that quotas of $700 per hour have been set for the Toronto district office.
The evidence is overwhelming, almost to the point where one could conclude that the Minister has misled the House, but that is not the responsibility of the Chair at this point. All the Chair has to be satisfied of is that a prima facie case has been made. There are two statements that have been made, one which the Minister knows of or should know of as the Minister in charge of the Department saying that there are quotas in the Toronto office, and the other made last December and not retracted by the Minister, that the only area in Canada where this practice existed was in the Kitchener office.
I have not heard in many, many years a more clear-cut case of privilege, a more clear-cut example of a prima facie case that the House is entitled to decide upon. Because that is the next question, as the Chair well knows. If the Chair finds that there is a prima facie case of privilege that does exist and that is constituted by the simple evidence before it, the question is put to the House. It is the House that makes the decision, not the Chair, as to whether there has been a breach of privilege and what should be done about it.
The Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe said that he is prepared to move the appropriate motion so that that question can be put before the House. I urge you, Sir, to reach the conclusion that there has been that kind of prima facie case established here to warrant the House proceeding with the matter further on the motion of the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe.

short-term and long-term interest rates from current levels does it predict if the deficit were (i) 0 (ii) $10 billion (iii) $20 billion?
2. What impact would the changes in interest rates have on the cost of servicing the national debt?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT DEPUTY CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEES OF THE WHOLE HOUSE
subtopic: IMPACT OF INTEREST RATES ON GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
1. Yes. (a) Not applicable. (b)(i), (ii) and (iii) Precise changes in short-term and long-term interest rates from current levels cannot be predicted unless the way in which the deficit is to be reduced to the specified levels is also indicated by the questioner. In general, however, lower deficits would influence interest rates downward.
2. The direct effect is clearly positive; that is, changes in interest rates lead to changes in debt servicing costs, in the same direction, given no change in the government debt portfolio.
Indirect effects of interest rate changes on national debt servicing costs can also occur. For example, rising interest rates may lead to decreased economic growth which, in the absence of policy change, would reduce government revenues and increase government expenditures, thereby raising the level of the stock of government debt or changing the composition of the government debt portfolio toward higher yield debt instruments. This would also increase the cost of servicing the debt.
A full response to the question would require consideration of the causes of changes in interest rates, over-all economic responses to these changes, and government policy and program reaction to both the direct and indirect effects of interest rate changes.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am told, Mr. Speaker, that I have only a few minutes left, although so much more can be said about medicare. However, let me try to conclude in these three minutes.
We were speaking, just before the House adjourned for lunch, of the alleged under-funding of the system. I have widely distributed the figures on that. I have not, like some of my provincial colleagues, forgotten the tax points, because to me it is money just as a credit card and a cheque is money. I would just like to say that for Canada on the average, for all of the provinces except two, we pay over 50 per cent of medicare. In the two provinces where we pay just below the 50 per cent,
we do so for excellent historical reasons. One of the provinces is British Columbia which always had the problem of far too many doctors imposing, of course, a much bigger burden on the system. I understand that the Minister in British Columbia is addressing that question right now. The other Province is Alberta where I believe they have a hospital in every village and in that sense the Province has overburdened its own cost a great deal. These problems are of some historical dimension and are totally provincial. There are provinces where we pay as much as 62 per cent and 58 per cent of medicare. Of course, when we say "medicare"-which is the word which has always been used-we mean buying for Canadians who have prepaid for it all of the expenses related to going to doctors and hospitals. That is what we mean. We do not speak of denticare or pharmacare. I believe I have always made that extremely clear to all Canadians. The $9 billion approximately which we transfer to the Provinces from all Canadians is exactly half of the total cost of what Canadians have given themselves as a society.
Therefore, in a nutshell, why should we have a new Canada Health Act? It is for a very simple reason. We do not want any overcharge. We do not want any direct charges for Canadians in need of health services, which are, however you want to say it, a tax on the sick.
I started my remarks by saying that it is with some regret that I am speaking on the second reading of this Bill. But it is also with some pleasure. It is with some pleasure because we anticipate now and can see the end to overcharges, extra billing and user fees on medicare. I am pleased because we Canadians in the medicare program-and 1 believe all Members of the House will agree with me-have in this program one of the best, if not the best, universal, top quality prepaid health care systems in the world, and we as a society have been wise enough to make it continue through the recession. This is what it is all about.

speechtext: We will now proceed with debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to address myself to the proposed Canada Health Act because it provides the opportunity to reiterate the perceptions and strong traditional support for the principles of medicare of the Progressive Conservative Party. There are times in the development of a country which stand out as landmarks of achievement. The evolution of our health system in Canada is replete with such landmarks. Many in this House and in the media have professed to be surprised at the support of my Party for the Canada Health Act. I know the Minister has expressed that same surprise. They should not have been surprised for the Bill is simply a consolidation of achievements which stand as landmarks in which we as Progressive Conservatives have participated.
More importantly, Mr. Speaker, the second reading debate allows us to discuss the future of health care in Canada with a view not only to enhancing medical and hospital care but ultimately to enhancing the health of all Canadians. That should be the primary objective which must be at the forefront of this debate and clearly in focus at all times. Neither partisanship not electoral considerations ought to cloud our vision and judgment in that respect.
Medicare is more than medicine and economics. Medicare is a service for individual Canadians and one of the critical bonds of Canadian federalism. Without it, we would suffer both as individuals and as a country. That is why our Leader has proclaimed medicare a "sacred trust". Our objective as a Party committed to medicare is twofold. First, we wish to fine-tune medicare through the legislation which is now before us so that the safety net serves as a trampoline which would boost Canadians to improved levels of health. Second, we wish to ensure that medicare remains and is strengthened as a bond within Canadian federalism and does not become either an irritant or a wedge between Canadians. Naturally, legislation alone cannot achieve that dual objective. Consultation, cooperation and responsibility among and between all participating governments, groups, individuals and health care professionals, is absolutely essential. Consultation and co-operation will allow everyone to feel that he has been part of the emerging consensus, and this in turn will result in a greater sense of personal and shared responsibility toward better health care. That sense of responsibility is crucial for two reasons: first, to ensure that health care resources are used effectively and efficiently so as to minimize costs and maximize benefits; second, to ensure that medicare remains a durable and lasting social program of which Canadians can be proud and confident.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we are convinced that non-partisanship, consultation, co-operation and responsibility, which we will exercise throughout this debate and thereafter, is required to enhance the health care system and the health of all Canadians.
Canada Health Act
There have been those who have said that medicare is slowly disintegrating, and the reasons for that can be varied. The Minister, for example, has said that medicare was in crisis and it was for that reason that the Canada Health Act would be introduced. But that disintegration, if it is there, is not disintegration, I suggest, because the Canadians are not committed to a universal health care program, but rather it is a result of the issues now facing the health care system. 1 would like to address a number of those issues today, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is important, when we look at the Canada Health Act, that we look beyond the narrow provisions of the Act to what is really facing the health care system.
To understand where we are and where we are going, and possibly even where we should be going is, I feel, absolutely essential in this debate. In order to do that, I point out to the House and to Canadians, such involvement in the medicare system by all levels of Government is useful only if a co-operative spirit prevails. In their words, Canadians rely "on the good sense of public health officials and political authorities ... to effect co-operation to work out an economical division of functions between the Dominion and the Provinces."
What I am referring to, Mr. Speaker, are commissions such as the Roweli-Sirois Commission back in the 1930s which laid the groundwork for co-operative federalism and for social policy. Although they might have been stated 50 years ago, it is absolutely critical that we do not forget those principles. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that although some people in this House might feel that from time to time we stress co-operation too much, I am absolutely convinced that there is no point in even discussing this issue if the bottom line is not the willingness to co-operate. I say frankly to the Minister that I think she would have progressed a lot further if she had shown that kind of co-operation from an early point. That co-operation is essential because we are a federal country. If that co-operation in an effort to win a battle is not there, however noble that battle might be or however noble its purposes, the possibility for co-operation in other areas will be jeopardized as well and thereby the harmony and unity in our country will be endangered.
I was deeply disturbed by the paper the Minister put forward this summer entitled, "Preserving Universal Medicare". Today she said it was not an attack on a specific province, namely the Province of Alberta. Any person reading that paper could not come away with any other conclusion than that the primary target of the Minister at the time was the Government and the people of Alberta and the health care system which they have in that Province. I intend to put a few remarks on the record today to show the commitment, not only of the Alberta Government but of its taxpayers, to a universal health care system in that Province.
When one takes a look at the Roweli-Sirois Commission of the 1930s it is important to see that it established another principle which has become part of Canadian life, that is, the matter of equalization. Equalization became a modus operan-

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
di between the provinces and the federal Government. In fact this was so much so that it was included in the Constitution. Premier Hatfield of New Brunswick was the principal spokesman on that issue. Not only did he want it to be the manner in which we operated in Canada, but he also wanted it enshrined in the Constitution. That becomes essential in this debate, Mr. Speaker. There are provinces today in Canada which are receiving well over 50 per cent not only of their health care budget but of their total provincial budget through federal transfer payments. As I have said to the Minister and to others before, those provinces, their premiers, their health Ministers and their governments are not mean spirited because of wanting to have either user fees or extra billing. That is not the point. The problem that they face is a lack of co-operation with the federal Government with regard to how they are going to fund a system. That is the point that they constantly make. I suggest to the Minister that after having equalization entrenched in the Constitution, it is absolutely critical that that principle never be violated, or that the war in which she sometimes seems to engage, never be used to destroy the health care system, especially in those so-called have-not provinces.
This has been the position of our Party, Mr. Speaker, since 1956 when delegates at a national convention in this city passed a resolution explicitly stating: "When contributions cannot be made and where need exists our principles will guarantee assistance of the state''. That was in conjunction with a national health care system. Our Party has a history of that commitment to medicare. It is that sense of commitment that allowed the Government of the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker to have endorsed the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of 1957.
There has been co-operation on this matter of medicare, Mr. Speaker, whether with former Liberal Governments or Conservative Governments federally or with provincial Governments of various political stripes. It is interesting that in 1961, still in the time of the Diefenbaker Government, a royal commission was established on health care services. We know what that royal commission stated. Again in 1979 the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) asked Justice Emmett Hall to study the health care system and to analyse fully whether the health care system was still meeting the objectives which had been determined by the founders at that time. I found that report interesting, and especially its title. It was called, "A Commitment for Renewal". I would suggest to the Minister today that if she looks at the Canada Health Act as a renewal she should not limit the renewal to the Canada Health Act only but extend it to other issues which we intend to raise in this debate.
Members who have been in the House for some time also know of the period which we went through when the debate on established programs financing took place and on those federal-provincial agreements in which changes from a so-called fifty-fifty cost share basis to block funding were made. It is my understanding, and I think the Minister would concur with this, that block funding is generally accepted by the provinces.
They also want to have a certain flexibility in terms of services which are now not generally insured services. In her definition of medicare today the Minister was very specific when she spoke of the 50 per cent, indicating that it will cover only the costs of medical care and acute care hospitals. I intend to address that matter more fully later on. There are Members on our side of the House, such as the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), who spoke during the time of the discussions on EPF and who were members of that task force. They will be stating our position relative to those debates as well.
The bottom line for us, Mr. Speaker, and we cannot emphasize it sufficiently, is co-operation. Not only was it stated in our own words, but I would like to quote for the record of the House the last words, so to speak, of Justice Emmett Hall in his report dated July 17, 1980. He said:
Finally, may I say I do not believe that a viable program can be expected or is even possible, based on the assumption that Ottawa can unilaterally withhold funds from a given Province which Ottawa thinks is in some kind of default.
The maintenance of the Canadian Health Services Program is dependent on continued co-operation between the Federal Department of Health and the Provinces. This co-operation is vital. Provision should be made for uninterrupted consultation. This could be achieved by the creation of a continuing committee consisting of the Federal Deputy Minister of a selected Assistant Deputy Minister and the Deputy Ministers of Health of the Provinces required to meet at least semi-annually and to monitor the Health Program continuously.
I see the Minister of Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) nodding her head in assent. I take it that that will also be a commitment on her part because it is absolutely essential that, no matter what is in existence in fact, that co-operative base remain. The Minister knows full well that she wanted to go to war with the provinces. She wanted to go to war with the health care professionals. There is no doubt in our minds that that was one of her objectives.
That is right, and it did not work.

This being the case, let us take a look at what now faces the health care system. When one takes a look at the percentage of the Gross National Product that is spent on health care it is interesting to note that Canadians spend a smaller percentage of their GNP on health care than our neighbour to the south. And Canadians should be justly proud of this. I think that is another reason why Canadians support the medicare system in Canada, although they might not have that figure at hand. For example, in 1971 the figure in the United States was 7.7 per cent and in Canada it was 7.5 per cent. Through the 1970s and early 1980s Canada's figure of about 7.5 per cent of GNP spent on health care remained relatively constant. In fact it clipped a little below that and then started rising. The last figures I have are for 1982. In 1982 two things happened. The American percentage of GNP spent on health care jumped to 10.5 per cent. In Canada it jumped to 8.4 per cent. We were and are still lower than the United States in those raw figures. I would like to make two points. Be it health care or any other social service, it can only be sustained and maintained with a healthy economy. The economy has seriously affected the ability of this or any other
January 16, 1984

government, or the provincial Governments, to maintain not only the system as we know it, but other programs that are valid as well. That is the first point that has to be made. As the GNP drops, these systems not only maintain their costing levels but in fact very frequently go up. That is the one point that I make. If there is any indictment which should be levelled against the Government, it is that its mishandling of the economy has seriously affected the ability of Canadians to maintain these health care systems.
Another point which must be made is that when one looks at the growing national debt in Canada, it reflects on these two figures which I have been using for the United States and Canada. The American 10.5 per cent does not reflect any part of their national debt as having been accrued through health care costs. However, a substantial part of the 8.4 per cent for Canada is health care costs. Therefore, the figure of 8.4 per cent as compared to the 10.5 per cent is not quite accurate. With respect to the debt, that cost factor has remained and is now a constant which is built into the system, and as a result of the economic mismanagement of the Government the ability for Canadians to maintain and in fact expand programs is seriously jeopardized because of the debt load they now face as a result of the actions of the Government. That is the other point which must be stressed.
I do not have time to pursue all of those factors but I know that others in my Party intend to do so. When we address the question of the Canada Health Act today, let us accept the principles but let us also critically examine the health care situation today. The principles of universality, accessibility, comprehensiveness of coverage, portability and non-profit administration are essential principles which we support. Therefore, we must be absolutely sure that we do not introduce contention either between the provinces and the federal Government or among the health care professionals, because I suggest that that contention can affect those principles detrimentally, resulting in conditions being breached and the very support on which the system depends being withdrawn. How ironic that by making an enemy of provincial counterparts in order to defend someone, one ends up making those who need the service most often the victims of that confrontation.
It is very interesting to note the Minister's defence with respect to the level of funding. It has been that the present level of funding of the federal Government for the health care system has always been maintained at 50 per cent plus and that in fact the Government is fulfilling its requirements under the terms of the agreement. I refer to Hansard of May 31, 1982, at page 17908 and an exchange between the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). The Member for Churchill was asking about the Government's commitment to extra billing and user fees and specifically whether there would be penalties attached to those two practices. In view of the Canada Health Act being before us today, I will quote the Prime Minister's answer. He said:
Canada Health Act
I put the question to the hon. member that the Constitution does not permit us to legislate in this area. We can only proceed by agreement. 1 have heard a member of the New Democratic Party shout across the way that we should withhold the money. If that is the position of the New Democratic Party, no doubt it would have effect. It would destroy medicare and extra billing with it.
After that answer of May, 1982, it is strange that we then have the Canada Health Act under these terms and that the Minister still states that her motivation was health care only and that politics, political consideration and electoral possibilities have absolutely nothing to do with her thinking on the Bill.
Our Party would like to see user fees and extra billing eliminated. That is why we are supporting the Bill. But in so doing we are saying to the Minister that she has an obligation not only to funding but to the health care professionals to treat them not only with the respect they deserve but to acknowledge the expertise they have and the service they are giving to Canadians. When I talk about health care professionals, I am talking about doctors, nurses, orderlies and people who are working and doing their very best in that system under the circumstances and with the funding which they have to give Canadians a health care system which is universally applauded.
I think it is important that we see these health care professionals in the best light possible. I have before me a paper that was written by a medical doctor, a general practitioner. He is a person who I know has studied the system very thoroughly. He says in part:
Physicians should realize that, while benefiting from an independent fee-for-service system of payment, that they also enjoy certainty of payment and ease of billing. On the other hand, governments should realize that provision for cost of living increases must be established which takes into account the net realizable income which physicians receive.
The fee-for-service method of remunerating physicians is frequently condemned and may not be perfect, but it may well be a less costly method of assuring medical care.
I know that Canadians, including physicians and nurses, do not like to take their salary disputes on to the picket lines. I say to the Minister and to those in the Department: once the Canada Health Act is passed do not use it as a cudgel against people who are legitimately trying to work within the system and do not use it as a cudgel to make them scapegoats in the health care system, because I do not believe that that is fair. Also, when we speak about the so-called funding process, it is strange that the Minister says that while she is supporting 50 per cent of insured services and that that funding is adequate, in the 1980 budget of the Minister of Finance the Government signalled, and the Minister stated that, that it was the Government's intention to cut, in the fiscal years 1982 to 1986-87, an amount equal to $5.7 billion from insured health care services. If the Government is cutting $5.7 billion over that period of time when we know that health care costs are rising at an average of 12 per cent plus per annum, how can the Minister then argue that she is still maintaining her side of the bargain?
While we want a national health care system, when one looks at the figures it is interesting to see the disparity in the amount of money that the provinces spend. I mentioned earlier that I thought the pamphlet entitled "Preserving the Universal Health Care" was an attack on the system in Alberta. For the

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
benefit of the House I note that the highest per capita spending on health care is in the Province of Alberta. In fact, that health care spending in Alberta is $1,013. Next in line, if we take a look at the figures, we see that Newfoundland's spending is $797; Prince Edward Island's is $735; Nova Scotia's is $832; New Brunswick's is $797; the Province of Quebec's is $884; Ontario's is $828; Manitoba's is $925; and Saskatchewan's is $889. 1 have mentioned Alberta. British Columbia's spending is $994; the Northwest Territories, spends $848 and the Yukon $734. While there are certain obvious disparities in terms of population distribution and in terms of specialists and so forth, the fact remains that certain provinces that are greatly dependent on health care transfers cannot afford the kinds of cuts which the Minister identified, namely the $5.7 billion, and maintain some of the expenditures that I have just read out. It is important we keep that in mind in this debate.
It is also important that this problem of funding has nothing to do, I would suggest, with partisan consideration. I know the New Democratic Party from time to time has campaigned, at least in my province and I am sure in other provinces as well, on the issue that that Party primarily is the defender of medicare.
It is interesting to note that the Province of Manitoba is running into the very same problems as governments in other provinces. I have before me-and I do not have time but I am sure somebody would like to devote part of his or her speech to it-articles that have appeared over the pre-Christmas and Christmas period in the Winnipeg Free Press under the heading "Hospitals in Crisis". These articles outline the difficulties which the New Democratic Party Government of that Province is having with the health care system. I am not suggesting to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) that the Party he supports and the Government he supports in that Province is not committed to health care. But I am saying to him and to all Members of the House that provinces are having great difficulty meeting the obligations, no matter what the philosophical commitment or stand on the issue is. As I said, I have before me a long list of articles that have appeared in Manitoba under the heading "Hospitals in Crisis". I will read some. They are headlines primarily that I will put on the record, but I will make the articles available to the House. These articles are based on the provincial Government's statement that it will increase health care funding to the hospitals by only 3 per cent next year. Just 3 per cent, that is all. There are good financial reasons for it. But I am saying to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill that he should take note of this issue in Manitoba. The opening paragraph of an article that appeared on December 21 reads, "About four people die each year in Manitoba while waiting for up to three months for open-heart surgery, doctors say." That is the first article. The headline of another one reads, "Experts warn of second rate hospital care". Another one which was published on December 23 reads, "Bed shortage cited in deaths of 4 patients". Another one reads, "Ceiling on funds posing difficulties." Another one, which is dated December 24, reads,
"Money is so tight at some Winnipeg hospitals that patients are being asked for the first time to bring their own Kleenex, soap, toothpaste, mouth wash and slippers when they check in". I do not mind that, Mr. Speaker. The reason I raised that for the benefit of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill is that back in a previous administration people used to talk about the menu being changed from three strips of bacon to two. I am just reminding the Hon. Member of what was said at some other point in time. Here is another headline, "For eye surgery, doctors say 'People going blind' waiting".
Here is another one that reads, "Intensive care beds short". I could go on and on but I think I have made the point. The point is simply made that the only way provinces are going to maintain the health care system is through co-operation and an absolute assessment of what is essential in that system.
Let me refer to the last Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker. What happened in the Throne Speech? Members of this House will recall that approximately $500 million additional were identified by this Government. It was an example of this Government's commitment to the health care system. It did not take Members on this side of the House and the media long to discover that the Government was obligated to pay that under the agreements it signed. Even 24 hours after that another $269 million was found on the road from Ottawa to Montreal. I say that the Government cannot argue that the health care system is healthy without addressing the question of funding. I said to the Minister when she met in Halifax in September with the health care Ministers that it was not helpful, not helpful at all, when she was asked to discuss funding of health care to have replied, "That is not my responsibility, that is for the Minister of Finance. I am only here to discuss health care". She walked out after an hour and a half and said it had been a waste of her time. That is not the way to go about things.
As my Leader stated back on July 1 in the riding of Central Nova, a PC Government led by him would restore co-operation and funding to the Canadian health system. That commitment stands and that commitment will be honoured.
Hear, hear!

As well, we are saying that when the next election comes, whenever the Prime Minister decides to call it, we will call a federal-provincial conference not to study again but to discuss with the provinces how the health care system is functioning and what funding should be examined, and the agenda will be open. We will be willing to discuss that agenda with the provinces and look at those issues and look at where extra money should be put in areas where they are not covered now by the cost shared arrangement. There are provinces which would like to get into alternate care. Some would like to try lower cost care programs, but they simply cannot do so because they are now strapped for the funding which they have to maintain for the present program. We are saying that not only is the agenda open but we intend to fulfil that commitment as well. I would suggest it is important to address it in that way, all of us knowing the provincial rights in this matter,
January 16, 1984

because of certain concerns that we have. In the remaining minutes I want to list some of them.
For instance, one of our concerns is the main demographic trend in Canada today, the so-called aging population. It is known that caring for the elderly is on average more expensive than caring for other sectors of society. But that trend has implications for the health policy. First, Canada must seriously explore the increased use of home care and nursing homes as alternatives to acute care hospitals. Right now, in a number of provinces in a number of hospitals 30 per cent of the acute care hospital beds-high cost beds-are being occupied by people with chronic disease or geriatrics. We must ensure an adequate supply of specialists and researchers in the field of gerontology. The challenge facing Canada and the testing degree to which we are a caring society is whether or not we can actively provide for not just the physicial needs of the elderly sick but attempt as best we can to address the emotional, the family and the spiritual needs of the aged and the dying. As well, and this must be a priority, we must find new approaches to improving care for Canada's natives. One just has to take a look at the statistics on infant mortality, on the reduction of life expectancy of Canada's native people, to know that this is an area that we must address much more seriously than we have in the past.
A closely related issue is that of preventive medicine. The goal of the Progressive Conservative Party is to move from what has necessarily been known as a sickness policy to a health policy. The economics of preventive medicine, while they cannot be fully known or accurately forecast, I suggest, give us enough incentive to pursue that issue very diligently. Neither can the rightness of preventing sickness by generating health be questioned. I know governments are sometimes a little leery of becoming involved in the area of lifestyle because of the imposition of Big Brother on society. However, I think all reasonable Hon. Members of the House recognize that that is not only good for society but has a very positive effect upon curbing health care costs.
On the matter of preventive health care, I can commend no one more on that issue, in bringing it to the attention of Canadians, than the Canadian Nurses' Association. The Association has pushed that issue. I have enjoyed its co-operation and the manner in which it approached the question of preventive health care. I look forward to further consultations with the Association.
Also we must take a look at the best economic use of our resources. In recent times health care economists have raised questions about the reasonableness of expecting that everyone who is sick should have access to the latest advanced diagnostic or treatment technology. One of the reasons we maintain that increased medical and technological research should be carried out in Canada is to increase the affordability and therefore the availability of such technologists and to keep them in Canada. That is important as well.
Adjournment Motion
Health care economists have expressed concerns-and they are shared by provincial governments, hospital administrators and others-that they must have the co-operation of provinces to control health care costs right in the hospitals. As a layman I know that sometimes that is dangerous territory on which to tread; I am not a health care professional. I say to the Minister and to the medical profession of Canada that we need their help, co-operation and expertise to maintain the health care system and to have cost reductions or at least to maintain the cost level at the present time so that we can generally afford the system.
At the beginning of my presentation today, I started by saying that our theme would be not only to preserve medicare but in fact to enhance it. I suggest to the Minister, with all the kindness I can muster, that in looking at the Canada Health Act and any regulations flowing therefrom we should not only look back or just look at the present; we must look at the future.
While this is a wide topic and obviously I would have liked to have more time, let me reiterate simply today-and some of my colleagues will make other points-that we support the principles which underlie not only Canada's medicare system but the Canada Health Act. Additionally, we want to see the debate expanded to address the issues which are really facing Canadians and the health care system.
We expect that co-operation not only from the Minister. In my discussions with health care professionals and with the provinces, everyone has pledged co-operation. All they are requesting in return is that they be heard, listened to, and that their expertise and experience be respected and in fact taken into consideration. That is our request as well.
