subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett)-National Revenue-Tax reassessment of small entrepreneurs; the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman)-Administration of Justice-Claim of influence exercised by Sidney Jaffe. (b) Legal residence of Sidney Jaffe; the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger)-Crown Corporations- Northern Transportation Company Ltd.-Request for investigation of management practices.

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-3, an Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to amend and repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, next month this Parliament will be four years old. For the duration of those four years I have served as the NDP health critic in the House. On the third sitting day of this Parliament, on April 17, 1980, I asked a question concerning the erosion of medicare. It was the first of dozens of occasions when I rose in the House on behalf of my colleagues in the NDP and called upon the Minister to do something to preserve medicare and to address the many problems which it faces.
That first year the Minister hid behind the fact that the Hall Health Services Review was not completed, and did nothing. When it was completed in September 1980, she then hid behind what she called the "complexity" of the situation for a winter until the Special Parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements was created in the spring of 1981. After it reported in August 1981 and seconded Justice Hall's call for action against extra billing by physicians and user fees, the time seemed ripe for action. The Minister could have responded to an active consensus against extra billing and by now we could have been putting our energies into the many other problems which medicare faces. Instead, she rolled over and went to sleep for awhile and let the then Minister of finance take over. The opportunity of concerted action by a concerned government against extra charges was ignored, and the politics of medicare were made even more complex by what followed.
In April 1982, federal transfer payments to the provinces under EPF were cut back. This aggravated federal-provincial relations concerning medicare and harmed medicare itself in so far as the cutbacks gave certain Progressive Conservative provincial governments philosophically hostile to medicare a political pretext on which to advance increased tolerance of extra billing, the reintroduction of user fees and the tying of benefits to high and rising health care premiums in British Columbia, Ontario and Alberta, something of which I warned the Government in the fall of 1981.
Most recently, only days before the introduction of the Canada Health Act, the federal Government further damaged the political context by trying to portray an automatic increase in its payments to the provinces as a discretionary response on its part to perceptions of underfunding and provincial concerns about the federal-provincial relationship over medicare.
This is the context into which the Canada Health Act comes after years of delay which between user fees and extra billing is estimated to have cost sick Canadians in the neighbourhood of $100 million just last year. Nevertheless, having long called for the federal Government to do something about the medicare crisis, we are pleased that the Government has finally tabled the Canada Health Act so that Canadians can see for themselves the extent of Liberal solutions to the problems which beset medicare. Despite the fact that the long-delayed Act comes into a political context which is not the best the Liberals could have contrived, we in the NDP will do our best to make the debate and the process which accompanies this Act an opportunity to do much more than what might be accomplished only by the Canada Health Act as it now reads.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has disappointed many people. After dangling the Canada Health Act in front of Canadians concerned about medicare for two years, the Minister had a responsibility to come up with a lot more than she has. In the days and weeks ahead I hope that we can not only improve on the mechanisms the Minister proposes for getting rid of extra billing and user fees, but that we can also get on with addressing other issues important to the survival of medicare.
The problems which beset medicare are at least fourfold, and this Bill deals with only one of the four dimensions of the problem. The four problem areas are: first, the need to clarify, strengthen and enforce the five basic principles of medicare as national health care standards; second, the need for the federal Government to re-open the federal-provincial funding relationship with a view to restoring a full federal partnership in medicare; third, the need to realize the full economic and ideological consequences of the fact that the economic climate which sustained medicare as a political compromise is no longer there and that new and deeper commitments to medicare will be required if it is to be preserved; and, fourth, the need to provide leadership and incentives for moving the health care model with which medicare currently co-exists away from the present physician-dominated, curative model, toward a more comprehensive, community-based preventive health care model such as groups like the Canadian Nurses' Association have suggested.
The Canada Health Act addresses only one of those four concerns, that is the concern about principles. It is a very important one and it is addressed through, first, the proposal to penalize provinces which continue to allow extra billing and/or charge user fees by withdrawing a dollar of federal funding for every dollar of such extra charges in any given province, and, second, the proposal to give the Minister of National Health and Welfare the power to determine discretionary reductions in the federal payment if a province fails to comply with any of the other program criteria concerning portability, universality, etc., or either of the two new conditions of payment-the provision of information and visibility.
We in the NDP are concerned with the dollar for dollar penalties for extra billing and user fees. Although we along with others, such as the Special Parliamentary Task Force on
January 16, 1984

Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements, have long called upon the federal Government to give itself more flexibility in responding to provinces which violate the principles of medicare by making itself able to gradually withhold portions of the federal Government payment according to the level of the offence in any given province, we never specifically called for dollar for dollar penalties. Thus, although we have long supported the idea of financial penalties for offending provinces, we have, complementary to our concern about the over-all political context into which the Canada Flealth Act comes, serious doubts about the effectiveness of the penalties proposed.
As a purely punitive measure, it may well be that dollar for dollar penalties are simply not tough enough to bring certain provinces into line. The penalty may not be great enough to be persuasive and may only be used as an excuse for more fed-bashing, for higher health care premiums, and for continued penalization of the sick through continued extra billing and user-fee charges. The $14 million that extra billing amounts to in Alberta is not a fiscal nightmare for the Alberta Government. It may well decide to absorb the cost of sticking to its free enterprise view of medicine, and in the meantime the actual extra bills for individual Albertans will be a burden on them.
This concern about the effectiveness of the penalties is further complicated by the fact that no positive incentives are included for provinces that want to respect the principles of medicare and want to act quickly. The only incentive is for violating provinces which are promised that at the end of three years following the inception of the Act, they will get all their withheld money back if they reform. If they have not cleaned up their act, the federal Government will pocket the money, thus creating another problem, which is that, under the terms of this Act, the federal Government stands to gain financially from continued extra billing and user fees. This is not exactly the highest moral ground that the Government could have sought. Why could not any money permanently withheld from an offending province be put to an appropriate health care use, provided that it was used in a way that did not offset the effectiveness of the penalties?
In recent weeks I have had the opportunity to meet and talk with representatives of a number of groups concerned about the Canada Health Act, groups such as the Canadian Health Coalition, the National Anti-Poverty Organization, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Nurses' Association, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Ontario Medical Reform Group and the National Federation of Nurses' Unions, plus several health care economists. I think it is fair to say that all of them are concerned about whether the penalties will do the job they are intended to do. Likewise, there were concerns expressed that the three-year waiting period given to the provinces to eliminate extra billing and user fees before they are permanently penalized may be too long, and they may serve only to delay a resolution of the question in various resisting provinces while making it more difficult for
Canada Health Act
those provinces which want to act quickly against extra billing. It has been five years since the SOS medicare conference in the fall of 1979. Why wait another three years and make it eight years before we finally have action against extra billing in those provinces where we most need that action?
To illustrate, a province might like to move to eliminate extra billing in the first year of the three years. What if it borders on a province which for one reason or another decides to wait until the end of the three-years, hoping perhaps for a more sympathetic federal government, a successful constitutional challenge against the Act or whatever? Practically speaking, the neighbouring province that moves quickly against extra billing in particular would bear a burden in terms of the fee schedules it would have to negotiate with doctors in order not to lose certain specialists to the province next door which was continuing to allow extra billing. Yet there is nothing in this Act for such a province. There is no positive encouragement or incentive for that kind of province.
All this is by way of saying that surely we can come up with a more creative and effective combination of negative and positive measures designed to truly eliminate extra billing user fees in a time frame that will see provincial governments having to take a position quickly. If, regrettably, some decide to carry on with extra charges in spite of all the provisions of an amended and improved Act, then the political process in such provinces will ultimately have to resolve the matter.
We will be suggeting a shorter time frame, a less generous stance toward those provinces that take their time or do not act at all, and a more generous stance toward those provinces that do show a willingness to respect the need to do away with extra billing and user fees. New cost-sharing programs with such provisions for initiatives in preventive and laternative health care models would be one way of encouraging them in their stand against extra billing and user fees, while at the same time such programs would address the question of federal under-funding and the need to reform the health care model. All of these concerns could be integrated. We will be providing more detailed suggestions in this regard at the appropriate time. We look forward to hearing from witnesses in the committee stage as to what they might suggest in this regard.
With respect to the discretionary power given to the Minister concerning perceived violations of other program criteria and conditions of payment, we are concerned about the incredible power seemingly thereby given to one person. Concerning extra billing and user fees, the provinces will at least know what they are getting into and what they are bringing on themselves if they allow these charges.
With respect to other principles and conditions, the same clarity is lacking in the Bill as it is now drafted. There is a concern that the Minister might be given final powers in this area which are inconsistent with the degree of co-operative federalism that medicare must continue to represent. We may be suggesting alternatives in this area when the Bill gets to the committee stage.
Parliamentary accountability for ministerial reductions in transfer payments was an idea that we proposed in our initial

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
response to the Canada Health Act. I was pleased this morning to see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare seems to have accepted that idea. She talked about having to come to Parliament if there were to be reductions in federal transfer payments so that the provinces would have the opportunity of a hearing. I was also pleased to hear her respond to provincial concerns about the wording of Section 12, (a), (c) and (d). That seems to be taken care of.
Lastly, as 1 have not seen the regulations at this point, I will be interested in the details of the demands made of the provinces with respect to principles such as universality, portability, the provision of information and the visibility of federal involvement in medicare.
We in this Party will be particularly interested in the provisions affecting universality and the collection of health care premiums. With universality re-defined upwards from 95 to 100 per cent, provinces like Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, which insist on paying a part of their health care costs in this regressive way will, we take it, be forbidden to deny anybody medical treatment on the basis of non-payment of premiums. These Governments, if they insist on making their people pay premiums, will have to find other ways of making people do this.
Incidentally, the existence of premiums in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, conveniently points out the ideological nature of so many medicare issues. It is the three richest provinces in Canada which cannot afford to abolish health care premiums. It is not a question of economics at all. It is a question of philosophy. In Alberta there is no gasoline or sales tax. They are not broke. For some strange reason they just prefer to tax the sick rather than drivers or consumers.
The Canada Health Act does not, as I said earlier, deal with the remaining three problems which face medicare; the federal-provincial funding question, the economic question and the health care model question. I would like to deal with these in turn.
With respect to funding, by remaining close-minded on funding, the Minister is still playing into the hands of those who falsely seek to justify extra billing and user fees by citing under-funding. Under-funding is a problem, a complicated problem, but user fees have never been demonstrated to generate significant revenue beyond the cost of collecting them, and extra billing only helps the self-perceived under-funding of a minority of doctors' income expectations and provides a morally dubious rationalization method for allocating scarce resources such as opportunities for elective surgery.
Medicare began to be threatened the day that federal-provincial cost sharing was abandoned in 1977 and bloc funding began. This ended direct federal involvement in health care decisions and put the federal government in a position where if it felt that a province was violating medicare, all it could do was lecture that province in public and hope for the best. The only other alternative under the 1977 legislation was to withdraw all federal funding from the offending province, an option which involves many known and unknown risks to medicare and which, as we know, was never used for that
reason. Indeed, an analogy comes to mind concerning the prospect of total federal financial withdrawal, that this really was the federalist equivalent of a nuclear deterrent, something only useful, if at all, as a threat but not as a sound long-term policy. It is out of that paralysis that the Canada Health Act comes.
In 1977 we warned the Liberals against the perils of bloc funding. At that time they admitted they were gambling with the future of medicare. They argued, however, that medicare was an established program that no one would tamper with. This was either an incredible display of political naivete about the nature of the political tensions inherent in medicare and the extent to which anything can be said to be established after only 10 years, or, more likely, it was a rationalization for the successful attempt by the Liberals to cap their contributions to medicare.
As I have said many times in the House, the federal Government made a major political error in the spring of 1982 when it unilaterally reduced the amount of money it had previously claimed it was providing to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education. The money attributable to compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee was consistently used by the federal Government in the period 1977-82, in its own calculations of what it was spending on health care. Those calculations were often self-righteously used to show that the provincial percentage spending on health care was declining in relation to the federal percentage. The removal of this money in 1982, of course, at first glance was a clever move because most provinces argued that it was not earmarked for medicare and post-secondary education and that it was unfair of the federal Government to regard it as such. When the tables were turned on the provinces in the fall of 1981 and their own arguments were used against them, one could hardly resist the temptation to conclude that the provinces had got what they deserved. Sophistry abounded and in order to know who was lying first you would have had to be at the table in 1977 when the deal was struck.
The provinces may have got what they left themselves open to, but Canadians in all provinces were dealt a triple blow in terms of medicare. First, they were treated to the spectacle of the federal Government arguing the provincial position and the provincial Governments arguing the federal position. There was a paucity of honest debate about what was going on. A veritable tower of Babel was created about who was funding whom at what level had been created and even the experts cannot sort it out now.
The provinces did suffer a decreased ability to pay for medicare in absolute terms as any withdrawal of funds from the provinces, whether earmarked or not, was bound to affect the provincial health care system. This is especially so in the case of Manitoba and Quebec where this was combined with a drastic and inequitable reduction in equalization payments as a result of the new formula established, again unilaterally, in April, 1982. Only the commitment to medicare of governments
January 16, 1984

like the present one in Manitoba has stood in the way of the effects of such cutbacks.
What is perhaps most important is that Canadians in medicare were dealt a blow by the federal reduction in transfer payments in that this unnecessary move by the federal Government provided the provinces with a handy political excuse for not responding to federal overtures concerning standards and further conditions for funding.
The Canadian medicare system was founded on a partnership, a federal-provincial partnership to establish and defend the right of all Canadians to an equally accessible, quality health care system, no matter where they lived in the country, no matter what their income. Both levels of government must stop pointing the finger at each other and stop engaging in manipulative number crunching. They must clean up their acts because all levels of government have a responsibility for what has happened to medicare so far.

Mr. Speaker, on the economic level, medicare is facing difficulties because the economic context in which it was created has vanished, probably forever. Like other segments of the Liberal welfare state, it was funded through revenues generated by economic growth rather than by a true redistribution of wealth or power in the Canadian society.
When the economy was buoyant, the Liberal Party could promote social reform while serving the business elite's values and economic interest. This is no longer possible, and to that extent the medicare crisis is the crisis of Canadian liberalism. In fact, judging by the way in which our Liberal friends will look after the future of that universal program, which is clearly popular and a source of pride for many Liberal supporters, we will know once and for all whether the Liberal Party is capable of maintaining our post-war social accomplishment.
If we allow medicare to disappear, all other programs will be at the mercy of those who contend, as most Conservatives do for instance, that social programs such as medicare, funded as they are through general revenue, are part of the problem rather than a part of its solution, and that we should revert to the days when social programs were more selective, that is more directed to the needy.
At best, those arguments reflect pessimism as to the will of the wealthy to permit a true distribution of their wealth, and reflect a real compassion for have-nots and a desire to more adequately meet their needs. For instance, it is sometimes suggested that the universal social programs have not changed the relative distribution of wealth and power. However, the left defended by those programs initially never thought they would change that distribution unless it was accompanied by fundamental changes in the economic system. What is apparent here is a kind of realism that had no basis in theory and that politically reflects a form of defeatism. At worst, those arguments come from a right that would have governments spend
Canada Health Act
less on social programs and transfer the costs to the various users. In this way, business would receive from government further tax breaks as incentives to invest and compensation for declining profits and rising competition for their products on the international scene, resulting not from lower worker productivity as many would have it, but rather from global economic conditions manipulated by the multinational corporations, whose freedom of action they would aggressively defend to the social and environmental limit of the economic model within which those corporations are now operating. [English]
In any case, Mr. Speaker, a choice is at hand for countries like Canada in the way they face up to the restructuring of the global economy, the intransigence of the wealthy at home and the attack on the economic viability of universal social programs. Are we going to determine Canada to be the kind of country in which the amount of sharing that is necessary to maintain programs like medicare, will be achieved through authentically progresssive taxation, or are we, as the Conservatives would have us do enthusiastically and the Liberals without as much fanfare, going to grovel before international market forces instead of trying to shape our own economic destiny in a way consistent with the social principles we say we hold and which we entrenched through programs like medicare? Now that times are tough our principles are to be tested and medicare will be a crucial test.
The pressures on medicare which can be attributed to the health care model which we find in medicare are all related to each other in so far as they cause greater and greater demands on a finite pool of money. As we have seen, for political and economic reasons it is an often dwindling pool of money.
There are three of these pressures which I should like to deal with, Mr. Speaker. Medicare is an ideological compromise between entrepreneurial medicine and truly socialized medicine. Thus, despite the rhetoric of the Canadian Medical Association about state medicine, doctors have actually had the best of all possible worlds. They and their patients have enjoyed their traditional freedom to pick and choose each other and to operate within a fee for services system, while at the same time they have been able to avoid all the risks of genuine entrepreneurship like unpaid bills. This is a fact which led some people, at the beginning of medicare, to say that medicare should actually have been called "doctorcare".
This compromise between the open-ended income expectations of those who think in an entrepreneurial mode and the unopen-ended nature of publicly funded programs has always been there and over the years has played a part, along with certain questions of principle for a minority of doctors, in the persistence of extra billing. The tension and the compromise have become even more tense with what some would argue is an increasing oversupply of doctors in some areas who are all trying to satisfy the same income expectations from the same finite source and with the widespread feeling among doctors that they are not being rewarded as generously as they used to be in comparison with other groups. These comparisons, how-

January 16, 1984
Canada Health Act
ever, always leave out the fact that their incomes rose abruptly with the introduction of medicare.
In any case, either by extra billing or by seeing patients more often than they really have to or, even worse and as has been documented, by doing unnecessary operations, doctors who are not happy with what their provincial plan pays them for a responsible, caring day's work in which the needs of patients come first, are able to generate more income for themselves, either consciously or unconsciously, whatever may be the case. If they do it by manipulating the market, so to speak, then they reap all the benefit of their marketing skills without the so-called discipline of the market place. The Government guarantees the fees of their captive clientele, and financial pressure on medicare is the result. If they choose to generate more income through extra billing, then the principles of medicare are endangered, and the threat of a two-tier health care system is increased, while provincial Governments which are not devoted to the principles of medicare see such extra billing as a welcome relief for the system and a handy way of passing on health care costs.
Analyses of extra billing which ignore this ideological tension in medicare and which, for instance, argue in its favour on the basis of the almost spiritual values attached to patient participation-which is the euphemism used for the cash transaction between doctor and patient-are a combination of psychological garbage and philosophical fluff which constitute an insult to the quality of relationships which all other health care professionals have with their patients. Furthermore, the whole argument is belied, in any case, by the often proven and nowhere denied relationship between the incidence of extra billing and the perceived adequacy of the most recent fee schedule.
A second pressure on medicare, Mr. Speaker, in the health care model is the increasing competition for funds caused by the advent of new medical technology and various life-saving surgical breakthroughs, such as transplants and bypasses and the expensive diagnostic and therapeutic equipment which goes with them. These demands have the advantage of being perceived as related to sensational successes, and also, of course, are genuinely important in an ultimate way to the patient and to the families who look to them for hope. But in a time of finite or diminished funding, whatever is gained on one front is often lost on another, and what is gained by the technological attention given to a limited number of patients may be lost in the attention not given to the care of the many who are not candidates for such technologies, or to the prevention of the conditions which create demand for those technologies in the first place. So increased over-all funding will have to occur if Canadians are to avoid having such difficult choices.
We in Canada must face up to the fact that we will need to have a debate on the allocation of health care resource and to move toward a system which is less physician-dominated and in which health promotion is as important as the treatment of
illness. Which brings me to the third pressure on medicare which comes out of the health care model, to which I have already alluded, and that is, the emphasis within the established model on the treatment of disease at the expense of disease prevention and health promotion. This emphasis is related to the role of doctors and the increasing role of expensive technology in that both the doctors and the technologies they are now able to employ tend to focus almost exclusively on the treatment of the sick. Thus, these three pressures complement and mutually reinforce each other. Under our present system, doctors are not paid for keeping us healthy. They are paid for treating us when we are ill.
Finally, there is the ideological dimension to the debate when it comes to medicare. The lip service which is paid to medicare by politicians from every end of the political spectrum has lulled a great many Canadians into forgetfulness of the real ideological divisions which existed about the idea of a publicly funded health insurance plan which sought to make good quality health care available to all Canadians. We need only recall that the two stages in the development of medicare both had to be pioneered by the CCF Government in Saskatchewan over great obstacles, fulfilling a promise which had first been made by the Liberals in 1919. But only when a have-not Province like Saskatchewan could do these things, did the federal Government feel that it could do no less. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, there remained long-standing tensions over this and the long-standing constitutional fact that health care was a jurisdiction of the provinces. That fact, combined with the ideological objection of many provincial governments against what they saw as socialized medicine, made for very difficult negotiations. Indeed, medicare had to be completed in stages from 1968 to 1972, as one by one the provinces responded to the fiscal mid-wifery of the federal Government. Governments today, like the Government of Ontario, are in direct political continuity with the Government which resisted the introduction of medicare in that Province, and that is something we ought not to forget. The jurisdictional and ideological tensions built into medicare simmered through the years of federal money aplenty, Mr. Speaker, but they are out in the open now and we have to deal with them.
Unfortunately, however, the ideological inclination of most provincial governments is not to answer the economic questions raised by the recession by going beyond the limits of the Liberal welfare state, but rather by trying to go back to pre-welfare state ethics and pre-welfare state economics. This is something we make no apologies for resisting when we hear those kinds of arguments offered. Instead of seeking genuine remedies to the under-funding problem which I have described, we see a happy coincidence of interest between the doctors and the provincial governments, neither of whom want to face up to fundamental economic questions or fundamental questions about the health care model.
Thus, not only do the principles of medicare need to be preserved, clarified and strengthened, but our health care system needs to be fundamentally reformed. The difficulty is in harmonizing thee two objectives. In the short run it contin-
January 16, 1984

ues to be a fact that the health care expectations of Canadians are determined by their familiarity with the present model. The increasing difficulty in funding these expectations is creating the situation in which those who do not support the principles of medicare are making headway. If health care continues to be the object of provincial and federal restraint and more and more Canadians have a negative experience of one kind or another with the availability of expected services, the enemies of medicare will get their way as more and more Canadians who can afford it demand to be able to pay for the kind of care which medicare is seen not to provide.
Before medicare, health care was allocated by the marketplace. Having it allocated by the bureaucracy or by the fiscal policies of Government is no great moral advancement, and we have to face up to that question. We are going to have to face up to these problems of funding, otherwise Canadians will eventually rebel against the allocation of health care resources by the bureaucracy and the enemies of medicare will be victorious. There must be, in the short run, expanded funding to preserve the principles of medicare and in the long run reform of the health care system. We hope that the debate on the Canada Health Act might be the beginning of such a debate and that some progress might be made even within the debate on the Canada Health Act in moving our health care system toward a more viable future. In this respect we welcome the support in principle which was quickly given to the Act by the federal Progressive Conservatives against the objections of PC Governments. Although we retain a healthy skepticism about the depth of their sincerity, we genuinely hope that their support of the Canada Health Act does actually reflect a new stage in their commitment to the principles and philosophy of medicare. We hope it is not just pre-election caution on an issue where that Party's traditional position is weak. May I say only half in jest that we hope it is not further evidence that under the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney) the Conservatives are becoming more and more like the Liberals every day, so much so that we now have to worry about the Conservatives moving into our territory on issues like medicare.
Oh, oh!

As the debate unfolds, Mr. Speaker, we will see more clearly. Meanwhile, let us work to preserve what actually may be an emerging national consensus against extra billing and user fees so that we can go beyond that to address some of the other problems which are facing medicare.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in the course of any such public debate about the nature of our health care system, all Canadians must face up to the fact that good health is intimately related to the social and environmental dimension of our lives. The strongest medicare principles imaginable, even in combination with a new emphasis on health promotion, will not bring all Canadians to the health potential which is really possible if we do not go beyond the individualized view of health care which we find both in the traditional health care model and in the newer emphasis on individualized prevention.
Indian Act
Healthy lifestyles are to a great degree limited by the constraints placed upon most Canadians by the social and environmental context in which they live. No amount of jogging or Fleischmann's margarine will counteract exposures to hazards in the workplace, malnutrition caused by inner city poverty or carcinogens in our food. Fundamental economic questions will have to be posed and pro-medicare people should have no qualms about asking such questions. Those whose economic interests are threatened by such questions are the same people who would resist the economic and fiscal reforms necessary to continue funding medicare within the five basic principles. Let the war, therefore, be waged on all fronts. We are not just fighting for a particular health care system. We are fighting for the total health, which can only be achieved as we achieve greater social, economic and ecological justice.
The Canada Health Act, after a substantial opportunity for concerned Members of Parliament to express their views on medicare should proceed to committee where we can hear from the public and then go about the work of amending and improving what, as it stands, is in so many ways a woefully inadequate response to the problems of medicare. The Government is well advised to be open to suggestions if it wants the continued co-operation of the New Democratic Party.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS
speechtext:
that Bill C-211, an Act to amend the Indian Act (loss of status), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today, Bill C-211, an Act to Amend the Indian Act, is certainly not a new one before the House. I had it as a Private Members' Bill before the House for much of the previous session. This Bill seeks to repeal what I believe is the most discriminatory and unjust piece of legislation which exists in Canada today. That is the infamous Section 12 (1) (b) of the Indian Act. This Section denies Indian status "to a woman who married a person who is not an Indian". As is well known, there is no similar restriction against Indian men.

January 16, 1984
Indian Act
For years most Canadians have recognized how unjust, improper and inequitable this particular measure is. But that same majority does not have to suffer the impact of this piece of legislation. We should be asking ourselves what it means in real human terms to those whom it does affect. It means that upon marriage to a non-Indian an Indian woman must leave the reservation, may not lease or inherit property on the reserve, must give up any property she already owns, cannot participate in band business, cannot have her children recognized as Indian and is prevented from returning to live with her family, even if she is ill, widowed or divorced. Finally, she loses the right to be buried on the reserve. All of this is because an Indian woman marries a non-Indian. The same thing does not apply to Indian men. There can be no more distinct example of officially sanctioned discrimination in Canada than this.
Let me personalize this situation even further by referring briefly to three individual cases which I think graphically illustrate the injustice of the present Indian Act. Jeanette Laval lost her status after she married a non-Indian back in the 1960s. In an effort to have this decision overruled she appealed her case all the way through the judicial system to the Supreme Court of Canada, without success. That Supreme Court decision denying her Indian status was rendered in 1973. At the beginning of 1984, 10 years after that decision was taken, Jeanette Laval, a full-blooded Indian by birth, is still waiting to have her status restored.
Given the outcome of the Jeanette Laval case, and knowing that the Canadian judicial system would not guarantee her rights, Sandra Lovelace, another full-blooded Indian by birth, formerly of the Tobique reserve of New Brunswick, tried a different route. She took her case to the United Nations Human Rights Commission on the basis of the discrimination which clearly existed in Canada. Her case was upheld in 1981 at Geneva. In effect what happened was that the United Nations Human Rights Commission told Canada to clean up its act. That was over two years ago, Sir, yet despite the international embarrassment that was caused to this country the Government has yet to act to address the problem of Sandra Lovelace and the many others like her. Sandra Lovelace too is still waiting.
A third well known case is that of Mary Two-Axe Early. She has fought long and hard. I know of no one who has fought more than Mary Two-Axe Early to gain full status for the many Indian women who have lost it over the years. Undaunted by numerous rebuffs and delays, she carries on that battle. I have great admiration for her work. Her anguish about the situation is clearly voiced in a comment which she made to me some time ago. She said: "It is easier for a dog to be buried on the Caughnawaga Reserve, my reserve, than it is for me, a full-blooded Indian who has been stripped of my rights". Mary Two-Axe Early is still waiting but she has almost lost count of the many years that she has had to wait.
Jeanette Laval, Sandra Lovelace, and Mary Two-Axe Early are just three of the approximately 8,000 Indian women who
lost their status in the last 20 years alone. It is estimated that something like 15,000 women have done so since 1920.
Let us not forget, when we are considering the loss of status of these Indian women, that what applies to the women also applies to their children. If the mother loses her status, then her children cannot ever become status Indians. It is estimated that almost 38,000 children have been affected due to the fact that their fathers are non-Indian. They are denied access to their ancestors' land, to their culture and to their traditions because of a law which was conceived and put into effect many years ago, not by Indian people, but by non-Indian bureaucrats and legislators.
These unacceptable statistics have been with us for many years. It is almost three years since the United Nations Human Rights Commission rendered its decision. That agency, one of the most highly respected international bodies, censured Canada because of the Sandra Lovelace case. Still the Liberal Government has failed to act. Years and years have gone by and it falls back on promises to correct the situation somehow, someday. It falls back on promises that it will act quickly and promises to guarantee Indian women their most fundamental human right. These promises, Sir, are rhetoric only. They are just so many words. There is never action to go with them. Legislation to correct this injustice has never been tabled.
The best, or perhaps the worst, example of this Government's lack of serious commitment to this measure arises from a statement that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back in 1981 after the decision in the Sandra Lovelace case was rendered by the United Nations High Commission. At that time the Prime Minister promised that within a year changes would be made to the Indian Act to eliminate all forms of discrimination. In other words, those discriminatory clauses would be done away with before the end of 1982. He made that clear promise in the House of Commons. It is now the beginning of 1984, and still we have seen no action. In fact, the very presence of this Bill before us today, almost two and one half years since the Prime Minister made that statement, proves that the Government is still dragging its feet on this matter while others are having to pay a terrible price, the loss of their most basic human rights.
To be fair, the Prime Minister is not the only one who should be blamed for this. There are, after all, other Ministers who do have some responsibility in this area. I refer, of course, to the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. Erola), who is here in the House, and to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). Like her leader, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women has been making promises in this field for a long time but without any action. But at least, I must say, this is one better than the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who just last month on the radio program "Our Native Land" said that he did not even list discrimination against Indian women as one of the legislative priorities which he included in his area of changes to be made to the status of Indians in this country.
January 16, 1984

With examples such as these before us, it is hard to believe that the Government is truly committed to do something about this and to reform. Of course, in the most recent Throne Speech action was once again promised. It was set out in the following words:
The Government will introduce a Bill to remove the longstanding grievance of discrimination against Indian women under the Indian Act.
Where is the legislation to deal with that matter? Why has the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development or the Minister responsible for the Status of Women so far not tabled a Bill to do what the Throne Speech said? If they were sincere, if the Government was sincere, if the Prime Minister was sincere when he said, in response to a question from the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), on December 12, just last month, that ending discrimination against Indian women would be a legislative priority, why has nothing concrete been done? Why has no Bill been introduced? I hope that it is not simply because the Government believes that the issue will simply go away, because it will not, or that it can easily and passively wait for Section 15 of the Charter of Rights to take full effect in 1985. Going that route would only bring about prolonged legal battles and further delay the removal of this discrimination. It is to prevent such a delay that this Bill is before us today.
I say to the government Members that if they are serious about eliminating all forms of discrimination against Indian women, then here is a Bill and a vehicle by which they can proceed. As a Government, they should take action now.
I would tell them that the previous Government had already moved, in the short period of time that it was in office, to take the action that this Bill contemplates today. The then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), said that if there was not an agreement between the Government and the band councils within six months, there would be unilateral action to remove Section 12(1)(6) from the Indian Act. That was a firm commitment which he made and not a vague promise.
That there continues to be a serious injustice created and preserved by the law of Canada in this part of the Indian Act cannot at all be denied. The evidence is incontestible. Its results are tragic. The first step in resolving this problem is before us today, to eliminate Section 12(1)(6). If the Government wants to go further than that and feels that other steps must be taken, then it can introduce those steps in committee. But most important is to give this Bill approval in principle today and to refer it to committee.
Since we all know how great an injustice this is, I ask that Members put aside partisan considerations and accept this Bill in principle and agree unanimously to send it to committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) for bringing this important matter before the House. I believe that all members who have studied this question will
Indian Act
agree that Section 12(1) (b) of the Indian Act epitomizes the injustice, racism and sexims of that Act. It typifies the whole patriarchal and colonial attitude that we had at the time that the Indian Act was first developed.
One can see three different ways in which Indian women suffer as a result of that Act. First, there are those women who married non-Indians and as a result of Section 12(1)(6) lost their status. As the Hon. Member pointed out, they lost their birthright and all rights to participate in the life of that Indian community even to the extent of being buried there. That is the first category of women who suffer from Section 12(1)(6), and perhaps they are the ones who feel it most keenly.
Other women have also suffered from this Act. There are those women who perhaps had hopes to marry someone who was not an Indian, but seeing that the application of this Act would have meant depriving them of their status as an Indian they decided it was too high a price to pay for that particular relationship. Therefore, they let go of the opportunity for that particular marriage, and in some cases this has resulted in a great deal of sorrow and disappointment.
Third, there is an increasing number of women who recognize that the provisions of Section 12(1)(6) will deprive them of their status. Since they do not want that to happen or to have their children deprived of status but want to have a relationship with someone who is not an Indian, they enter into a relationship which does not involve a recognized marriage. There are still situations in Canada where this involves some kind of social stigma both for themselves and their children. This is the kind of suffering that should not have to take place.
This Bill should not have to come forward as a Private Members' Bill. It should have been the subject of a Government Bill. Action has been promised time and again but nothing has happened. For example, on December 7, 1982, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) appeared before the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government and when he was asked about the Government's commitment to remove this discrimination, a commitment which we have heard many times before, he said, "We intend to move with considerable haste on this question". He said that he was preparing a Cabinet paper on this question for his colleagues to study. What does "considerable haste" mean for this Government? Obviously it does not imply what ordinary people understand by "considerable haste" because we have not even seen a Bill.
Due to the complexity of this issue I have asked the Minister to table a Bill at the earliest opportunity so that Indian governments, Indian women's organizations as well as Members of Parliament and members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development can study it and appreciate the different ramifications that will be involved in the Bill.
I do not believe that the kind of Bill brought forward by the Hon. Member is really the answer. There are too many complexities involved. Therefore, we need a chance to study this and make sure that it covers all of the bases.

January 16, 1984
Indian Act
The Throne Speech promised such a Bill but again the Minister indicated on the radio show Our Native Land that this was not one of his priorities. When I pressed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on this subject on December 12, he said that it was a legislative priority, but the fact is that we still have not seen the Bill. We still have nothing before us from the Government side to which we can react. I believe that this question is important enough that the Government should give it the very highest priority so that we may deal with it. It will require some time both in the Committee and in the House. It is not something that can simply be pushed through in a matter of a few hours or days. It affects too many people and too many communities.
I want to see some legislative commitment to this question. I sat as a member of the subcommittee which studied Indian Act discrimination against Indian women. I think some of the things it said must be emphasized. In our final report on page 39 we pointed out that a straight removal of Section 12( 1 )(b) implies retroactivity back to the beginning of the Act. Unless there are amendments to the contrary, an amendment would permit the addition of children, grandchildren and great grandchildren.
There are a number of questions involved in this question of retroactivity. First, there is the question of reinstatement of those women who lost status. We know this is not universally acceptable by Indian bands and Indian governments. Some Indian communities oppose it very strongly. Other Indian communities are on record as saying it should happen right away and that these women should be reinstated. Indian people are not unanimous one way or another on that question. In my view and in the view of my Party these women who were born as members of a certain Indian community have a right to continue as members of that community. Marriage should not have altered that right. It is a birthright, it has to be respected and any law that denies a person her birthright is an unjust law and has to be changed.
Our Party will support measures that lead to reinstatement of those women who lost status by virtue of the action of Section 12(1)(6). At the same time we say that we have to recognize the poverty that occurs on many Indian reserves and the shortage of land and homes on most Canadian reserves. Many Indian people have expressed concerns to me about this.
I think this Parliament has to recognize the need for an enlarged land base and an enlarged financial base for Indian communities. People have said that money should not stand in the way of justice. I agree. I believe there are two sides to that statement. First, as far as Indian leaders and Indian communities are concerned, they should welcome back their sisters and their daughters without regard to their financial needs. These women have a right to belong to those communities, and I believe Indian leaders should be open to receiving them back as members. They are part of the family. This is one side of the statement that money should not stand in the way of justice. The more important side as far as this House is concerned is that the federal Government on behalf of Canada
has an obligation to make money available so that Indian communities will not be further burdened by the addition of more people when their resources are already very tight. There is a housing shortage on Indian reserves. When there was talk about possible action to remove this section of the Act, there was a rumour that some housing money would be made available to provide homes for reinstated women. There was a concern expressed by other people on the reserves, who in many cases are living in deplorable housing conditions, housing conditions that every Canadian should be ashamed of, that perhaps giving housing money to reinstated women would mean that they would lose their right to get a home.
I believe the federal Government has to recognize the need that it is dealing not only with individuals but also with communities. The federal Government has to tackle the problem of Indian poverty head on and make money available not only for homes for reinstated women but make housing money available for all those people who at present are living in deplorable and substandard housing. There is a need for large sums of money. Section 12(1)(6) was not an Indian law. It was a law imposed upon the Indian people by non-Indians, and I believe the non-Indian Canadian public should bear some of the burden and Indians should not have to bear the full burden of reinstatement because of a law imposed upon them.
Our Party supports reinstatement of those women who lost status. But what of their children, their grandchildren and their great grandchildren? In many cases it would be very desirable for these people to have Indian status. Certainly many of them would like to have status as Indian people. They would like to be part of the community of their grandparents, for example. However, it is one thing for us as a Parliament to reinstate people who once had membership in a band, women who were born into the Indian community. It is something else for us to give membership to people who never have been members. This is not an easy question for us to determine. I believe, perhaps, this question is not really ours to determine at all. 1 believe there is a right of Indian communities, bands and governments to determine their own membership criteria in accordance with international covenants.
While we support the concept of reinstatement of Indian women who lost status, we cannot give a blanket support for the reinstatement of their children, their grandchildren or their great grandchildren. What we do support is the idea that all first generation children of Indian women who lost status would have status as Indian people without necessarily being attached to Indian bands. Indian status would give them the right to have their names placed on a general list. They would be eligible for certain federal programs, and if the bands developed membership criteria that were non-discriminatory, that allowed for the reception of these people into membership, then they would go with our blessing. I do not believe that we as a Parliament have the right to say that these people will automatically be accorded membership. We believe bands have the over-all right and responsibility to develop their own criteria as to what constitutes membership. Many bands in the last couple of years have taken that step and have developed
January 16, 1984

their own citizenship criteria-their own membership codes. In most of the cases that I have seen these have been non-discriminatory. We need to recognize that what is necessary to some bands in southern Canada is not necessary or desirable for Indian people in northern Canada. Different Indian peoples in Canada have different, membership needs. It is important there be some flexibility, that our Government recognize in Indian governments the possibility of developing different membership codes among different Indian nations. I think our Government's responsibility has to be limited to ensuring that these codes are in accordance with international standards and that they do not discriminate on the basis of sex or marital status.
Finally, we believe there has to be an appeal body established to decide on matters of disputed membership. There are different mechanisms by which this could take place. The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government has recognized some of the complexities involved in this. It recognized that there has to be some degree of reinstatement. It also recognized that Indian bands themselves, Indian Governments, Indian nations, have the right to determine their own citizenship criteria and that the basic unit for determining that should be the band as it is newly constituted, including the reinstated women who once had status and had it denied.
In conclusion, I am in support of the basic intention of this Bill. However, 1 wish the Government would be more forthright and would not only say that it will act but indeed will act and will bring in a Bill which can be studied in the House and in Committee and will provide an end to that discrimination.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be speaking today, now that the House has resumed sitting in the new year. Interestingly, the matter of native rights is being raised for the first time this year. Mr. Speaker, before getting down to basics, I may say I have the impression that the Bill being presented in the House by the Member for Kingston and the Islands has the agreement of Members on all sides of the House as far as principle, wording and expectations are concerned, and I think we all share the desire to eliminate discrimination on the basis of sex from the Indian Act.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the agreement expressed by these two Members, is shared entirely by the Government. The only difference at this point is a matter of time, of weeks. I would like to make it clear right away that this was included in the Throne Speech read by the
Indian Act
Governor General. It is understood that the matter of native rights, the matter of equality among the sexes will be maintained, that is, it is made quite clear in the Throne Speech that the Government will soon act on the report by the Parliamentary Committee on Indian Self-Government. It will table a long-awaited Bill aimed at deleting provisions of the Indian Act that discriminate against Indian women. It will provide for funds to maintain job creation programs on the reserves.
Mr. Speaker, the Private Member's Bill presented by the Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) is the same kind of Bill presented during the last session on adoption, income supplements and unemployment insurance benefits. The proposals were made in a private Bill, and only three weeks elapsed between the time the Bill was tabled here in the House and our reply.
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of Hon. Members and of Indian women who are the people most directly concerned, here again it is a matter of weeks, not months but weeks. The important thing is that we shall have an opportunity to check it over time, Mr. Speaker. I think the Member for Kingston and the Islands will see the case settled in about eight weeks, since the Hon. Member has already raised some very basic problems.
The principle being defended by the Member for Kingston and the Islands is quite clear and it is to eliminate discrimination on the basis of sex. I could not agree more, there is no problem as far as that goes, but as the Hon. Member who spoke earlier pointed out: What are we going to do with the people who have been affected by this form of discrimination? The Bill presented by the Hon. Member fails to mention a series of problems that will have to be solved by the legislator. The only action proposed in the Bill is to abrogate paragraph 12(1)(6) of the Indian Act. Nothing more. There is absolutely no mention of what we will have to do with the people who over the years, over the past hundred years, have suffered as a result of this discrimination. And that is an important point as far as the principle of justice is concerned.
So we must make a distinction between two things, Mr. Speaker, in the Bill presented by the Hon. Member. First of all, the Government fully agrees with eliminating discrimination on the basis of sex, but second, there are also a number of elements that need improvement, and subsequently, if we look at this in greater detail, we must consider the impact of the changes to be made in the Indian Act.
Mr. Speaker, here is the kind of question the Government will have to answer before changing the Act. What are the rights of Indians who marry non-Indians? What are the rights of children born of such marriages? Anyone who has natives in his constituency is well aware of the advantages and privileges but also of the constraints on Indians who live on the reserves.
Those are some of the factors which ought to be considered before we amend the legislation. Some questions should be asked: What will be the rights of children born from such marriages? Will the first, second and third generations enjoy

January 16, 1984
Indian Act
the same privileges? What happens in subsequent marriages with persons who have not been Indians for one, two or three generations? Will band councils always agree to consider those people as Indians? With respect to that factor, Mr. Speaker, the major difficulty has often been to know just how long one remains an Indian after marrying an Indian. I have no intention of going into generic considerations, but that has often been at the root of the problem. Except that, in keeping with Indian traditions, more often than not the rights belonged to the men, which raises the issue of discrimination, but still, Mr. Speaker, we must keep in mind the whole Amerindian tradition. The role of the legislator was not to steer the evolution of mentalities.
The riding of Manicouagan is home to eight Indian bands, Mr. Speaker, they do not always see eye to eye and it is now difficult for the Indians to reach a consensus on full recognition of the rights of men and women, but the evolution is fast enough when it comes to recognition based simply on the equality of individuals rather than the difference in sex.
I would like to emphasize one of the major factors, Mr. Speaker, namely that mentalities vary considerably among Indians, depending on the reserve where one happens to be. Indians who live in the core of a city or close to a significant concentration of white people have a different way of thinking. However, Indians who still live in extremely traditional regions have a way of thinking which is altogether different from ours, as white people, Mr. Speaker. The Department of Indian Affairs should take that factor in very serious consideration before making any change whatsoever.
I would like to remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that the Subcommittee which examined this whole question received briefs and representations from various native groups who were naturally not unanimous on how the Indian Act should be amended. I do not think that the legislator could unilaterally decide on the amendments to the Indian Act. This in no way contradicts what the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands is proposing, Mr. Speaker, except for the fact that this problem had to be examined more thoroughly and extensively even though we have always recognized the principle advocated by the Hon. Member.
Earlier, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) asked some pretty basic questions. What is important is not simply to amend the Act, but rather to correct certain inequities and ensure that there would be a uniform system once the Act had been amended. I asked only two questions, but many others come to mind. For instance, what are the rights of Indians who marry members of another band?
I should point out to Hon. Members that I am regularly in contact with the Indians of my region and that, for those who know them, the Montagnais are not Hurons and the Hurons
are not Iroquois and the Denes are not Inuit. For the Indians, this notion of belonging to a band and its designation as such is extremely important.
In this regard, I would like to underline an important fact, namely that we have a tendency to consider the problem as though the Indian people thought as we do, which is a basic mistake. As a white man and as a politician my thoughts are exactly those of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, However, I must say that before speaking for the Indian people, I always ask for their opinion. Before speaking about this bill, Mr. Speaker, I therefore wanted to know the position of the Indian leaders, and I express their views very carefully because this issue is also important to them.
We must do a good job of representing those for whom we speak, when we represent the Indian people, it is very easy to mix our prejudices or simply our ideas with some of the concepts in which the group we represent believe. I thought it important to point this out. This is why I noted this afternoon how happy the Inuit people of my constituency were to see someone like Mr. Charlie Watt appointed to the Senate to represent them properly because there are major differences in the way of thinking of a white man and of an Indian, which takes nothing away from the fact that rights should be recognized and Indians should be allowed to give their views on the matter. I have here extremely revealing letters received by the Department about whether or not we should now recognize the principle of equality among the Indian people, even though the Department has already taken position on this issue after coming to an agreement with the Indian people as the result of lengthy consultations. The delay now required simply concerns formulation of the Act. As of January 9, 1984, seven days ago, Mr. Speaker, 87 bands had asked to be exempted from application of Paragraph 12.1(b), which deprives Indian women who marry non-Indians of their status. However, 298 bands have asked to be exempted from Paragraph 12.1(a), which deprives from their status at the age of 21 people whose mother and paternal grandmother were not born status Indians.
Without wanting to contradict the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, with whom I and the Government agree completely, we must point out that we are dealing with individuals and not with volumes, areas or quantities, but rather with a certain mentality, certain traditions and the respect of the individual. You are contrasting collective rights with individual rights. We must therefore be very careful about how we amend an Act which will apply not to the Hon. Member, but to other people, because this bill concerns people who have a very specific environment and a special way of thinking and who are very proud of some of their traditions. For the benefit of Hon. Members, or people who may be listening to such comments, I would like to say that when you visit the Band councils and try to apply to the Indian and Inuit people solutions which are appropriate to the white man or to
January 16, 1984

city dwellers, you find that native people do not completely agree with us, and I want to point this out because, in my constituency, we do not apply the same solutions to the Montagnais people of the Lower North Shore as to the Montagnais of Schefferville or the Inuit of Fort Chimo. Now, for the benefit of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, I should like to mention that we have in Schefferville the Montagnais reserve and the Neskapi reserve, which are approximately six miles apart, but the way to administer Neskapi affairs is quite different from the way to administer Montagnais affairs. And the way the Montagnais live in Sept-Iles is quite different from the way the Montagnais live in Saint-Augustin. And the Inuits in Fort Chimo live differently from the Inuits in the New Quebec Territory. Mr. Speaker, these differences which stem from very old traditions among North American Indians must end, but they must end while respecting the people who will be affected. Mr. Speaker, this new approach is the result of years and years of efforts, and we see changes every day. Mr. Speaker, at the departmental level, we must take into account the views expressed by the band councils, by individual Indians, men and women, and as I was saying, the amendments which will be introduced in a few weeks will not be rash.
These amendments are the results of a series of questions which have been raised by the Hon. Members who have spoken before me and by various people who are involved in the defence of rights and freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that when this government put forward its Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it had taken into account all the problems and issues addressed by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. But there exists no quick remedy to these problems, because one must deal very carefully not only with individual cases, but also with the people affected.
Mr. Speaker, before suggesting amendments, the Department has had to find answers to other questions. For instance, what are the rights of non-Indian spouses? It had to address these questions before drafting amendments to the current legislation. What are the rights of a child whose parents belong to two different bands? As you can see, we had to look into this before drafting amendments which would affect the private lives of these people. That is important. You are dealing here with people and traditions. When we consider the past, we realize that we can do things in 1984 that could not have been done 50, 25 or even 10 years ago. It is a matter of evolution.
From the white man's point of view, Mr. Speaker, we can see that there are inequalities, but before we deal with them and amend the legislation, we must try to foresee the consequences. Also, Mr. Speaker, we are often anxious in this Parliament to blame this or that party. 1 simply want to say this: the Penner report required hours, days, weeks and months of analyses before being finalized. This is an extremely lengthy
Indian Act
process, and we know quite well that those who really know the Indian people could have made similar recommendations even before the committee began its work. However, in the name of democracy and of respect for human rights, we had to hear all interested parties before finalizing recommendations which will have to be acted upon during the coming months. That is the important thing.
The principles contained in Bill C-211 sponsored by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands are recognized by the Government. There is no problem in this regard. However, the Government had to go much further to ensure that, by amending the Act, we would not cause other and worse problems than those being denounced. This is important because, once the Indian Act is amended, there will have to be a series of legal and financial compensation measures applicable to those who were victims of discrimination throughout the years. Therefore we could not improvise. Indian men and women as well wanted and wished for such a change, but from the point of view of white people, it could have happened more quickly. On the other hand, the native people wanted balanced measures through which men and women would again be guaranteed full rights while removing distinctions because of sex.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, looking at native people in other lands, we realize that we have had to face a similar problem, namely a problem of traditions. And you know, Mr. Speaker, that the native people are not the only ones to resist changes. It is exactly the same with white people, but some political decision has to be made eventually. As I have already said, such a decision will be made within a few weeks, and will see that the Indians will be pleased with the Bill and with the compensation granted to the victims of discrimination.
Before concluding Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind you that when we legislate on individual rights as opposed to collective rights, we should be extremely cautious because it is quite easy to be high-handed. We are now considering a Bill which seems hardly controversial because it tends to remove sexual discrimination, but there are others which bring individual rights and collective rights into conflict. One of the basic reasons why Parliament should discuss such issues is that it would be quite easy to be high-handed. And what 1 would object to in the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands is that it merely states the principle and does not consider all the consequences of that principle in terms of enforcement and compensation of the individuals concerned. While endorsing the principle of the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, we on this side of the House will deal with the matter to make sure that a compensation is granted so that all Indians will be satisfied once the Bill is tabled. When I speak of Indians, I refer to both men and women. They will all agree with the terms of the Bill and its new implementation.

January 16, 1984
Indian Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, since the time allotted to us has expired, I will merely add before concluding that we will not vote today for the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member and that very shortly she will vote for the implementation of her principle and several other fine procedures for the benefit of the native people.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INDIAN ACT REMOVAL OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN-LOSS OF STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard 20 minutes of the same old stuff. We have had promises and promises that something would be done about this terrible situation. I should like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary that on August 4, 1982 the House gave directions to the Standing Committee to strike a subcommittee to look into this issue. That subcommittee comprised seven Members from all Parties in the House, a member of the Assembly of First Nations, a member of the Native Council of Canada and a member of the Native Women's Association of Canada, so all the major Indian organizations were represented. The Parliamentary Secretary went into great detail and claimed that all kinds of things have not been studied and so there are no answers. He raised the question of what will happen to the Indian children. All that has been addressed by the subcommittee in its unanimous report to the Standing Committee, which was presented to the House on September 20, 1982. It has been languishing ever since. I do not believe the Parliamentary Secretary when he says that this is going to be resolved in eight weeks. The answers are here.
When the Minister appeared before the Committee he said that the Government wanted to complete the review with recommendations for amendments that would eliminate sex discrimination from the Indian Act. All those things were done, Mr. Speaker. For instance, the subcommittee recommended that children of mixed marriages should be granted Indian status and, furthermore, that the first generation children should automatically become members of the band of the Indian parent. The subcommittee also recommended amendments that would permit Indian women and their first generation children who lost status under Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act to regain their status immediately upon application, and so on. It also raised the question of band control of band membership. These matters have also been addressed by the Committee on Indian Self-Government.
There is no need to study the matter any further. Mary Two Axe Early has been working on this since 1965. The testimony that she gave to the Committee would make one weep.
I am not going to say any more about this, Mr. Speaker, as it has been well covered today. I will sit down and watch Hon. Members opposite squirm around and talk it out.
