subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF SMALL ENTREPRENEURS
NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF SMALL ENTREPRENEURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last month I had the opportunity to raise an issue in this House concerning the treatment of the Department of National Revenue of small businessmen and small part time farmers in this country, and others who I suggested were being treated less than fairly by the Government. I was in the process of asking the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) how his Department was going to respond to certain circumstances which the unfair treatment of taxpayers by this Government was creating.
The particular situation to which I refer is that many taxpayers in this country are now having their tax assessments reassessed and are now being asked to go back four years, five years and six years and pay taxes on deductions which had been allowed in previous submissions to National Revenue. As a result, a great many of these people have been put in grave financial danger. They have been strapped because of the demands put on them. It has been extremely difficult for these people to stay in business.
As you can understand, Mr. Speaker, any new business starting up, unless it is very fortunate, is bound to encounter a period of time during which the operation is not going to be profitable from the point of definition of the Government. This is so with any new and growing company or entrepreneurship. It is something we normally expect in our system. However, it seems to be the intention of this Government that a business must be profitable from the very outset and, indeed, if it does not show a profit, then it is not going to be allowed to claim expenses.
What this has done, besides driving a number of people out of business because of the demands on their bank roll and on their pocketbook, is stifled ambition in the country. Because of the unfair practices of Revenue Canada there are now people who will just not take the chance or the risk of attempting to start a business. This is an unhealthy attitude for any government to be creating in the country. Certainly, this country was founded on the free entrepreneurial system and I believe that any move on the part of this Government to stifle and put down that entrepreneurship is certainly not a good thing.
I am concerned today, Mr. Speaker, that I will not have an answer to my question for the people in this country who have been afflicted with this obsession of the Government to gouge them to the degree that it has forced them out of business. My question, however, is quite simple. What happens to these companies who, in the meanwhile, do become profitable? Is the Government going to turn around and tell them that it obviously made a mistake in the past and should not have reassessed them for those five or six years causing all this money to be paid out in back taxes, and will therefore return all of that money that it has gouged out of them during this past year? Or is it going to turn around and say, "We have already determined that you were not going to be a profitable business and we have disallowed your expenses in the past so now, under those circumstances, we are going to allow you to keep all the profits you make without charging you any tax on

January 16, 1984
Adjournment Debate
those profits"? No, I think not, Mr. Speaker. We are not going to have any clear answer to those questions today, and the reason we are not going to have a clear-cut answer is that this Government does not have the answer.
This system is contrary to our basic British parliamentary heritage. The Government has made you guilty until proven innocent. It has burdened this nation with a monetary burden which is totally unfair. If you want to take your case to court you have to pay a lawyer in order to do so, and in most cases, as they quite blatantly point out on all of the material with which they provide you, they will not necessarily be liable for any fees that are imposed on you, the taxpayer, in order to justify this wrong that they have perpetrated. Mr. Speaker, they scare most people to death.
The taxpayers in this country have been yipped by this Government. In case the Government does not know what yipping is, fishermen off Grand Manan will tell you that when they haul a fish up off the bottom which they want to use for lobster bait they just take that fish and yip it; in other words, turn it inside out and throw it into the bait bag. That is what the Government has done to the taxpayers of this nation. Besides stifling the incentive for this nation to grow they have been yipping the taxpayers. Mr. Speaker, this is a wrong which this Government has perpetrated in this country, a wrong which this Government should make right, but will not.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF SMALL ENTREPRENEURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is seeking an explanation of the way in which the income tax law is applied when a person declares business losses and in return seeks to offset these losses from taxable income from another source, such as a full-time job. Before the deduction of such losses can be allowed there are a number of questions that might have to be asked about such a return. Are the expenses reasonable in the circumstances? Were they in fact laid out to earn an income? Are they all related to the business or are some of them wholly or in part of a personal nature, such as would be the case when an automobile is used for personal non-business purposes and for business purposes as well? The most fundamental question when losses from a business are being claimed is whether or not the taxpayer can really be said to be engaged in a business. There are a number of ways of assessing this fact.
When the Hon. Member first raised the question in the House, as he did again today, he spoke of people being assessed for the last five or six years. He should know that reassessments going back more than four years are not allowable under the Act except in circumstances involving fraud, which I would suppose are not the circumstances he is talking about. Moreover, even though the law would allow reassessments covering four years, the assessing guidelines of the Department make numerous exceptions so that the period is often shorter.
There is another point to be made. The law places limits in some cases on the loss that may be claimed from a farming
enterprise even where it may be established that a farming business has been carried on. I will not go over what must be a familiar ground to many Hon. Members other than to say that where the taxpayer is mainly engaged in some other occupation, though engaged in farming as well-and I admit that this is a gross oversimplification-the limit on the loss which may be claimed for a year is $5,000.
Finally, there could be circumstances in which the losses are originally disallowed because there was no expectation of profit, and it could be appropriate to reopen some of the years reassessed because later years did show a profit.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-CLAIM OF INFLUENCE EXERCISED BY SIDNEY JAFFE. (B) LEGAL RESIDENCE OF SIDNEY JAFFE
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-CLAIM OF INFLUENCE EXERCISED BY SIDNEY JAFFE. (B) LEGAL RESIDENCE OF SIDNEY JAFFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Sidney Jaffe has been involved in legal proceedings in New Jersey, Nevada, California, Florida and Canada. He was convicted of contempt of court in New Jersey and was later abducted by bounty hunters on behalf of a Florida bail company. Before I start today, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that that was a reprehensible, indefensible action and an affront to Canadian sovereignty. On that issue I have no reservations whatsoever. I concur with the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) in his answer to my question on December 19. The international law does not include the right to seize people from other countries. The matter of extraterritoriality and the seizure is before the courts. On that issue I have no question.
The issue I raise is the question of application and the granting of Canadian citizenship to Mr. Sidney Jaffe that seems so clearly to be a matter of convenience. That is demonstrated by the following timetable.
In the Spring of 1977, Mr. Jaffe moved to San Francisco, according to a court transcript of his own testimony. On June 13, 1979, a bankruptcy petition was filed by Mr. Jaffe in San Francisco. On July 19, 1978, at a trial in San Francisco, Mr. Jaffe states in his testimony that his residence was in San Francisco for the previous two years. On August 7, 1980, on a bail bond application, Mr. Jaffe lists his address as 1000 Green Street, San Francisco, for the previous three years.
On January 19, 1981, there was an application for Canadian citizenship and also an application to regain his driver's licence, and he stated in his application that he had stayed for 150 days outside of Canada in the previous four years, which is obviously incorrect according to all of the testimony that has been brought forward.
In April of 1981, he jumped bail posted in the United States by the bail bond company. On May 18, 1981, information was filed on failure to appear and a capias was issued; that is, a warrant for his arrest was issued. On June 17, 1981, he became a Canadian citizen under Section 5(1). Mr. Jaffe's licence was given back to him after it was revoked for non
January 16, 1984

payment of fines for 1978. He became a citizen on June 17, 1981. It is very difficult to understand how residency could have been intended or met under these circumstances.
In a letter dated March 23, 1983, from Nevada State Senator Bill Hernstadt to the Florida Parole Commission, he stated that he objected to Mr. Jaffe's release on parole based on his previous experience with Mr. Sidney Jaffe in Nevada. He said:
In my opinion, he has an almost congenial compulsion to steal from customers, shareholders, friends and associates for his own selfish ends.
-Sidney L. Jaffe is a congenital thief and his white collar crimes can wipe out a family's savings just as completely as a hardcore criminal with a firearm. If you do release him he will return to Canada, sail his yacht at the Toronto Yacht Club, and laugh in the faces of his thousands of victims who are paying for his luxurious and glamorous lifestyle.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney), in speaking in his first speech in the House of Commons spoke of the value of Canadian citizenship or what the value of Canadian citizenship should be. He rose in the House in October, 1983, and gave a glowing maiden speech in which he talked about the quality of Canadian citizenship. He said "We have come through so much together-against overwhelming odds-that our citizenship has become a privileged symbol in our lives." He went on to attribute our respect for the rule of law and our respect for neighbour and property as a cornerstone of our valued citizenship. How sad it is to see this citizenship besmirched.
In the United States, circuit court Judge Perry said:
In Canada, Jaffe is hailed as a fellow of the Yacht Club, a patron of the ballet, in Canada he's hailed as Joe Nice Guy. But in the U.S., Sidney Jaffe is nothing but an economic predator. Mr. Jaffe is plain and simply a crook and he didn't get a damn thing he didn't ask for . . . He's guilty as hell.
I am quoting a judge of the United States court.
In the Canadian courts, just after Christmas, Judge Di Cecco said he was fed up with Mr. Jaffe's "skating" in the witness box and that it had become abundantly clear that there were gaping contradictions in Mr. Jaffe's testimony. He then went on to warn Mr. Jaffe's lawyer that Mr. Jaffe should be notified regarding his potential for perjury.
Mr. Jaffe's lawyer in the United States court said:
Jaffe (would) use his influence to stop the Canadian criminal prosecution of Putnam County public officials resulting from the kidnapping.
Mr. Jaffe claimed that his influence was with the Canadian ministry of External Affairs.
What does all of this add up to? To me it indicates that amendments to the Citizenship Act in 1975 were inadequate and inappropriate, injuring and cheapening the value of Canadian citizenship. The currency of Canadian citizenship has been debased to a level of Canadian passports known internationally amongst criminals and terrorists as flags of convenience to travel internationally and carry on with their scurrilous deeds. The Citizenship Act, its regulations and administration disgrace hardworking Canadians who worked for five and three years to qualify for something they felt had high value, Canadian citizenship. It is now debased. It is now no more than a flag of convenience.
Adjournment Debate
Where was the investigative process of the Citizenship Court in this case? Where was the investigate process of the Justice Department in that in spite of the overwhelming volume of court and public documentation available the Minister of Justice proceeded with Mr. Jaffe's defence without apparent in depth knowledge of Mr. Jaffe's character and background as identified in the documents I have mentioned?
Will the Minister attempt to protect Canadian citizenship laws by prosecuting under the Citizenship Act with the same zeal that he has prosecuted for the protection of Canadian sovereignty? Or, in fact, is there something behind the allegations of influence? Will the Minister identify with whom and where in the Justice Department or the External Affairs Department does this alleged influence lie?
Mr. Jaffe is not the problem. It is the system and his manipulation of the system that exposes the system's inadequacy and therefore the inadequacy of the law and of the political and governmental system that administers and creates it. The Minister may wittingly or unwittingly be co-conspiring to make the law and Canadian justice not only appear to be but in fact to be an ass. Mr. Jaffe gained citizenship, a citizenship of convenience. At the same time we find that the reigning world champion bobsledder, a Canadian immigrant, comes to Canada, works to become an Olympic athlete, a champion for Canada, yet because he is competing for Canada for gold he cannot gain Canadian citizenship on the same basis. I conclude with the question, why is it that our Olympic athlete cannot gain citizenship on the same basis as Mr. Jaffe? Does he not have influence?

I can say nothing further which will assist the Member in understanding what Jaffe's Florida lawyer had in mind when he wrote the letter the Member referred to. subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LTD -REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
CROWN CORPORATIONS-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LTD -REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15, I rose in the House to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) a question regarding the management, safety and accounting practices of Northern Transportation Company Ltd. and about concerns that a conflict of interest existed because employees and managers of NTCL are also directors and shareholders in a competing company in marine transportation in the North. Since then I have not received a direct answer from the Minister, although he indicated at the time that he would look into the matter.
I have furnished the Minister with the required information he needs to begin his investigation into the operations of NTCL. As well, I have placed a number of questions on the Order Paper respecting my concerns in regard to this public company.
To assist the Minister, I would like to expand somewhat on my earlier questions. First, regarding management practices, there is sufficient evidence that management is involved in questionable contract arrangements with various companies,
for example, a 400,000-tonne tug in Tuktoyaktuk for which there does not seem to be any need. NTCL is stopping its operations in the Athabasca region, yet there is business there. In the Churchill operation, a number of items have been bought which have questionable value or use in that area. As well, the company's profits have decreased from about $8 million in previous years to about $1.4 million in the most recent year.
Contractual arrangements have been made involving a northern welding company in Hay River. At the same time as NTCL lays off its welders for the season, within a matter of weeks it is hiring welders through a private company in the area. The welders of NTCL are very concerned about this.
Also, it would be good if the Minister would explain to the House why NTCL has failed to obtain a multi-million dollar contract in recent years and why, after it had failed, Arctic Transport Ltd. was called in by the company and awarded a contract to complete the contract because there was insufficient material for the successful bidder to finish it. At a time profits are decreasing to the company it would seem to me it should be an active bidder for work.
NTCL has a contract with the United States air force to deliver fuel and other goods for operations in the North, particularly to the Pine Tree line, and to other areas as well. It has a contract to operate a floating drydock owned by the United States air force, referred to as ARD-31.
Could the Minister verify that NTCL is operating ARD-31 for its own business and other purposes which are prohibited directly by the contract it has signed? Would the Minister ask for a copy of the contract and table the information in the House so that I and others could use it? Would the Minister check if this drydock is also being openly offered by NTCL to companies for service this year?
In terms of safety, the Minister is now aware of the numerous hazards which exist relating to fuel handling, fuel shipping and cargo handling on the Mackenzie River and the Beaufort Sea. The most pressing concern relates to the unsafe practice of shipping dead cargo on fuel barges and operating combustion engine vehicles on barge decks where explosive fuel containers are still on the below deck. Certainly these practices are not in accordance with Coast Guard regulations. In fact, insurance companies are unwilling to ensure fuel barges which are used to haul dead cargo, yet NTCL persists in these practices. I am concerned that if these proper safety procedures and practices are not respected, there may be a serious accident in the North.
These cargo-laden fuel barges travel to many communities in the North. They are docked and used as floating piers for other barges, which greatly increases the potential for serious consequences such as an explosion or a major fire. That is why it is important to investigate these safety practices.
I would also ask that there be an investigation as to whether proper equipment and training is available to employees who are operating in these areas and on these barges. It is impor-
January 16, 1984

tant for the Minister to inquire about the operation of this floating drydock in order to ascertain precisely how much cash flow is being generated by NTCL while operating the drydock over the last four years.
Regarding conflict of interest, why is it that this Crown corporation is operating without any guidelines or direct accountability to its shareholders, the people of Canada? I have information which shows that upper management and middle management officers of NTCL own shares in a private company which is in direct competition with NTCL and marine transportation in the North. In fact, a superintendent for NTCL operations and contracts is a member of the board of directors of the company as well as a shareholder.
Is it the policy of this Government to allow senior management people who are employed with taxpayers' dollars, despite their positions within a Crown corporation, to invest in a competing company? If it were in the private sector, they would be down the road so fast it would make their heads spin.
Accountability is an important issue with regard to Crown corporations. They should not be privileged creatures free of the exigencies of private business environment, yet protected from public scrutiny. The Minister, through the privilege of the office entrusted to him, is the representative of the majority of shareholders of NTCL, the people of Canada. Therefore, it falls upon his shoulders to guarantee that the companies are efficiently and effectively managed to best serve the public interest and not just private ambition. The Auditor General has stated this over and over again in his recent reports. He did so just recently in a speech wherein he suggested that the political officers of this country, Members of Parliament, ought to look into this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-NORTHERN TRANSPORTATION COMPANY LTD -REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the comments of the hon. gentleman opposite on the subject of the Northern Transportation Company Ltd. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we are satisfied that NTCL is well managed and carries out its business in a safe, efficient manner. I would like to go over some of the general points made by the Hon. Member in order to demonstrate the secure foundation for our confidence in NTCL.
The Hon. Member questions the management practices of the company. I remind him that the management now in place has taken NTCL from a position in 1975 before recapitalization in which it lost over $5 million, with a $2.5 million net deficit in shareholders' equity, to a position at the end of 1982
Adjournment Debate
in which the company earned $4.7 million on revenue of $47.5 million and had shareholders' equity of $35 million. Retained earnings at the end of 1982 were more than $9 million. Furthermore, while accomplishing this feat the company continued to provide the high quality customer service for which it is justly renowned. The management of NTCL should be complimented for the success it has achieved.
The Hon. Member questioned the safety record of NTCL. I can assure him that the company has an enviable safety record. NTCL has a full safety program for its employees, including comprehensive training in the handling of hazardous materials. The company's record in preventing industrial accidents, oil spills and other safety-related incidents is one of which it and we can be proud. Not prepared to rest on its laurels, NTCL is continuing to improve its safety-related procedures and training.
The Hon. Member raised the issue of NTCL's accounting practices. I am surprised at his suggestion, particularly in view of the fact that NTCL's auditors are Deloitte Haskins and Sells, a respected firm of chartered accountants in Edmonton. That firm, which has been involved in the audit of NTCL accounts for several years, reported favourably in NTCL's 1982 annual report. In addition, the Hon. Member might not be aware that NTCL was the subject, several years ago, of a comprehensive audit by the Auditor General and Deloitte Haskins and Sells. I am happy to report that the Auditor General gave NTCL a clean bill of health in his report of March 31, 1982.
The final point raised by the Hon. Member relates to a purported conflict of interest involving company officers. No director, corporate officer, or manager of Northern Transportation Company Ltd. is a director of Arctic Offshore Ltd. There is a second line supervisory employee, working at NTCL's Hay River marine maintenance base, who is currently a director of that company. This employee has no control or influence over the awarding of NTCL business, or over solicitation of business or relations with NTCL customers.
I trust I have been able to reassure you, Mr. Speaker, and the Hon. Member, that our confidence in NTCL and the way in which it carries on business is well founded.
